5. Inference

Prefill, decode and the arithmetic of serving tokens

Serving a language model is two different workloads: a parallel prefill pass and a sequential decode loop. This module covers decoding algorithms, the KV cache, batching and parallelism, and how extra inference-time computation buys accuracy.

Printed pages: pp. 203–245

Learning outcomes

  • Separate prefill from decode and explain why the cache exists
  • Compute top-k, top-p and temperature transformations by hand
  • Estimate KV-cache size for a given model shape and context
  • Reason about latency, throughput and inference-time scaling

Common misconceptions

  • ❌ The KV cache is a speed optimisation that changes nothing about the output. ✅ It is an exact reuse of the keys and values of earlier positions. It changes the cost of the computation, not its result.
  • ❌ Prefill and decode are two stages of the same work. ✅ Prefill is one parallel pass over the prompt with quadratic attention. Decode is one token at a time against the cache, with linear attention per token.
  • ❌ A lower temperature makes the model more accurate. ✅ It makes the output more concentrated. The entropy falls and the mode becomes more likely, but nothing about what the model knows has changed.

Lesson 13. Prefill, decode and the KV cache

Two workloads, one model

Estimated study time: 28 minutes

What you will learn

  • Distinguish the prefill phase from the decode phase
  • Explain what the KV cache stores and how it changes the cost of each new token
  • Compute cache memory for a given model shape and context length
  • Describe prefix caching and continuous batching at a conceptual level
  • Compute the acceptance probability of a speculative-decoding draft and the expected tokens per verification pass

The ideas

  • Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and fills the cache.
  • Decode generates one token at a time, reading the cache instead of recomputing it.
  • Serving throughput is dominated by memory bandwidth and batch scheduling, not only arithmetic.
  • Speculative decoding verifies a cheap draft in one parallel pass; the output distribution is exactly the target’s.

Practice

Q. What is the essential difference between prefill and decode? — concept

  • ✓ Prefill processes all prompt positions in parallel; decode generates one token at a time using cached keys and values
  • Prefill is done on a CPU and decode on a GPU
  • Prefill uses a different vocabulary
  • Decode does not need attention

Why: Both phases use the same weights. Prefill is one large parallel pass; decode is a sequential loop that appends to the KV cache.

Q. Without a KV cache, generating token t requires recomputing keys and values for all t−1 previous tokens. What does caching change? — concept

  • ✓ Per-token work becomes approximately linear in the context instead of quadratic in recomputation
  • The model becomes non-autoregressive
  • The attention mask is no longer needed
  • The vocabulary shrinks

Why: Caching stores K and V once per position, so each new token computes one query against the cache — a linear read instead of a full recomputation.

Q. Two requests share the same 2,000-token system prompt. What does prefix caching save? — concept

  • ✓ The prefill computation for the shared prefix
  • The decode computation for new tokens only
  • The need for a KV cache
  • The tokenizer pass

Why: The cached key/value tensors of the shared prefix are reused, so only the differing suffix must be prefilled.

Q. A service receives a long document and a short question, and generates a short answer. Which phase dominates the cost, and what would change that? — transfer

  • ✓ The prefill dominates: the document is read once, quadratically, and the decode over the cached document is cheap. Fewer tokens, or reusing the cache across questions about the same document, are what change it
  • The decode dominates, because every token is generated one at a time
  • Both cost the same, because the model has a fixed cost per request
  • Neither matters, because the cost is the number of parameters

Why: Prefill is parallel and compute-bound; decode is sequential and memory-bound. A long prompt with a short answer is a prefill problem, and the ways out are the ones that touch the prefill: fewer tokens, a cheaper read, or reading the document once and reusing the cache for every question about it.

Go and do it

Step a toy transition model forward one token at a time and inspect the context, the chosen token and the local entropy at each step. Open Autoregressive decoder in the llm-foundations-lab application.

  • §5.2.1 Prefix Caching · p. 223 — Reusing cached prefixes across requests.
  • §5.2.2 Batching · p. 223 — Batch scheduling and its effect on utilisation.

Further reading

  • Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference (2022) — Analytical treatment of the prefill/decode trade-off.
  • Kwon et al., PagedAttention / vLLM (2023) — Memory management for KV caches.

The words this lesson uses

  • Prefill — Process the prompt in parallel
  • Decode — Generate one token at a time
  • KV cache — Stored keys and values for past tokens
  • Prefix caching — Reuse a shared prompt’s cached state
  • Continuous batching — Admit and retire requests every step

Lesson 14. Decoding algorithms

Greedy, beam, top-k, top-p and temperature

Estimated study time: 30 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute temperature-scaled softmax probabilities by hand
  • Apply top-k and top-p filtering and renormalise the surviving mass
  • Explain the diversity/coherence trade-off in each method
  • Predict how a seed and the sampling parameters interact

Concept Decoding is a policy on top of the model

The model produces logits; the decoder decides how to turn them into a choice. Greedy decoding takes the argmax, beam search keeps several partial sequences, and sampling draws from a modified distribution. None of these change the model — they change which of its plausible continuations you see.

$$\Pr(y_i \mid x, y_{$\tau$ rescales the logits before filtering, so it interacts with **top-k** and **top-p** rather than acting independently. A small $\tau$ concentrates the mass; a large one flattens it.

Concept Two ways to truncate the tail

*Top-k* keeps a fixed number of candidates. It is predictable and simple, but the right $k$ depends on the shape of the distribution: too small and the output is repetitive, too large and implausible tokens re-enter.

*Top-p* (nucleus) keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches $p$ . When the distribution is peaked, that set is small; when it is flat, the set grows. The candidate count therefore adapts at every step.

$V_i = \left\{ y_i^{\text{top}1}, \dots, y_i^{\text{top}k_p} \right\}, \qquad \sum_{j \le k_p} \Pr(y_i^{\text{top}j}) \ge p$

In both cases the surviving probabilities are renormalised so they sum to one over the pool — otherwise the sampled distribution would be defective.

Greedy and beam, fairly

Greedy is reproducible and never wanders, which is what you want for structured output. Beam search explores several hypotheses but tends to favour short, high-probability sequences unless you calibrate length, and it spends $b$ times the compute per step.

Concept Determinism and reproducibility

Sampling is only reproducible if the random stream is. Seeding the generator makes a run replayable: the same configuration produces the same tokens, which is what allows a bug report to be reproduced and an experiment to be compared against a baseline.

Two independent streams from the same seed produce identical sequences — the lab shows both, side by side, to make that concrete.

Filtering arithmetic, step by step

Work through one configuration by hand.

$\Pr'(y_i) = \frac{\exp(u_{y_i}/\tau)}{\sum_{y_j \in V_i} \exp(u_{y_j}/\tau)}, \quad V_i = \text{top-k} \cap \text{nucleus}$

  • 4. Renormalise over the pool: masses should sum to 1 → 1.000000 .
  • 5. Draw $r \sim U(0,1)$ and walk the cumulative distribution.

A real model would recompute the distribution after every token as the context grows. Here the distribution is held fixed so the effect of the decoding parameters is isolated.

Entropy across temperature

Computed from the current logits at the current top-k and top-p.

As τ grows the distribution flattens and entropy rises; as τ shrinks it approaches greedy decoding.

Worked example

From logits to a sampled token

Take the default logits $[4.2, 3.4, 3.0, 2.2, \dots]$ with $\tau = 0.5$ . Scaling multiplies by 2, giving $[8.4, 6.8, 6.0, \dots]$ , and the softmax of that puts $0.7580$ on the first token, versus $0.4876$ at $\tau = 1$ and $0.2835$ at $\tau = 2$ .

Now apply the filters: with top-k = 4 and top-p = 0.9, the lab keeps 4 candidates, whose probabilities sum to $1.000000$ . The draw itself is just a walk along that renormalised cumulative distribution using one uniform number.

The ideas

  • Decoding is a policy on top of the model distribution; it never changes the model.
  • Top-k fixes the candidate count, top-p fixes the candidate mass.
  • Temperature rescales logits before filtering, so the two interact.

Practice

Q. Logits [2, 1, 0] with temperature τ = 0.5. What are the probabilities? — calculation

$\Pr(y_i) = \frac{\exp(u_{y_i}/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(u_{y_j}/\tau)}$

  • ✓ [0.866, 0.117, 0.016]
  • [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]
  • [0.960, 0.039, 0.001]
  • [0.5, 0.3, 0.2]

Why: Scaling by 1/τ = 2 gives [4, 2, 0]; softmax of that is [e⁴, e², 1]/(e⁴+e²+1) ≈ [0.866, 0.117, 0.016].

Q. What distinguishes top-p from top-k? — concept

  • ✓ Top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p; top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens
  • Top-p is deterministic; top-k is random
  • Top-k uses logits; top-p uses probabilities only
  • They are identical operations with different names

Why: The candidate pool size is fixed for top-k and adapts per step for top-p, although the mass threshold p is constant.

Q. In the course’s sampling laboratory, which is true of the base (temperature 1) distribution shown in the chart? — concept

  • ✓ It is the raw softmax of the logits and does not change when you move the top-k slider
  • It changes whenever the seed changes
  • It is renormalised after top-p filtering
  • It is the distribution actually sampled from

Why: The base distribution is a property of the logits alone; filters act on the temperature-scaled distribution and produce the final renormalised one.

Q. What is the effect of temperature on entropy? — concept

  • ✓ Lower temperature reduces entropy; higher temperature increases it
  • Temperature does not affect entropy
  • Higher temperature reduces entropy
  • Entropy only depends on top-k

Why: Dividing logits by a small τ sharpens the distribution (lower entropy); dividing by a large τ flattens it (higher entropy).

Q. The same model has to emit a valid JSON object in one case and a varied story in the other. How do the three knobs differ between the two jobs? — transfer

  • ✓ The JSON wants a sharp distribution with the tail cut off; the story wants a flatter distribution with the tail kept, so that the unlikely continuations stay reachable
  • Both want a sharp distribution, because precision is always better
  • Both want a flat distribution, because variety is always better
  • Temperature is the only knob that matters; top-k and top-p are the same thing

Why: The three act on different things. Temperature reshapes the whole distribution and keeps every token reachable. Top-k cuts the tail by count. Top-p cuts it by mass, so how much is cut depends on how peaked the distribution already is. A task with one right answer wants the tail gone; a task with many right answers needs it.

  • Greedy decoding — Always take the most likely token

Lesson 15. Efficient inference and inference-time scaling

Serving costs and spending compute to think

Estimated study time: 28 minutes

What you will learn

  • Relate context length, batch size and precision to memory pressure
  • Explain output ensembling and search scaling as ways to spend inference compute
  • Distinguish measured latency from an analytical cost model
  • Choose a decoding configuration for a given accuracy/latency target

The ideas

  • Inference-time scaling trades tokens and calls for accuracy.
  • Search and ensembling need a scoring or verification signal to be useful.
  • A cost model explains the trade-off; only measurement proves a speed-up.

Practice

Q. Best-of-n sampling improves an answer only if: — concept

  • ✓ Some scoring or verification signal can distinguish better candidates
  • n is a prime number
  • The temperature is exactly 1
  • The model’s context window is empty

Why: Extra samples expand the candidate set; selection needs a signal, otherwise the choice is arbitrary or returns to the model prior.

Q. The course’s KV-cache and attention figures are described as analytical models. Why is that stated explicitly? — concept

  • ✓ Because they estimate cost from formulas; only measurement on real hardware proves a speed-up
  • Because the formulas are wrong
  • Because caching has no effect on memory
  • Because benchmarks are forbidden

Why: Analytical accounting shows how cost scales with shape and configuration, but real latency depends on hardware, kernels and scheduling. Distinguishing the two keeps the claim honest.

Q. A team turns on a setting that spends ten times the compute at answer time, and the answers come out the same. What has the setting bought, and what would have been worth buying instead? — transfer

  • ✓ Nothing: the extra compute was spent without changing the answer. What pays is a change in the answer — usually by searching over candidates and verifying them
  • Better answers, because ten times the compute is ten times the knowledge
  • A shorter answer, because more compute is more efficient
  • Nothing, because inference-time compute never helps

Why: Inference-time scaling is only worth its cost when the extra compute changes the output. The interesting work is on the diversity of the candidates sampled and the quality of the verifier, not on the length of the chain. Ten times the compute that produces the same answer is ten times the bill.

Go and do it

  • Inference-time scaling — Buy accuracy with extra computation at run time
  • Beam search — Keep the best b partial sequences
  • Verifier — A scorer that judges candidate solutions
  • Throughput — Tokens served per unit time

6. Reasoning

Spending computation to reach answers, not just tokens

Reasoning appears when a model writes intermediate steps and when training rewards them. This module treats reasoning as search plus verification, then covers process supervision, scaling training for reasoning and how to evaluate it honestly.

Printed pages: pp. 247–278

Learning outcomes

  • Explain reasoning as search over intermediate steps
  • Compare best-of-n sampling, beam search and verification
  • Describe outcome supervision versus process supervision
  • Recognise the open questions about memorisation and evaluation validity

Common misconceptions

  • ❌ More reasoning tokens mean the model reasoned more carefully. ✅ Token count is a cost, not a measure of quality. A longer trace can be wrong in more places, which is why the cost-adjusted protocol exists.
  • ❌ Outcome supervision trains the model to find the right step. ✅ It penalises the whole path, so the model is left to guess which step caused the failure. Per-step labels remove that guess.
  • ❌ A higher pass@k means the model is better. ✅ pass@k measures whether any of k samples is correct, which is a property of the sampling budget as much as of the model.

Lesson 16. Reasoning as searched computation

Prompting, sampling paths and verification

Estimated study time: 30 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define reasoning operationally as producing intermediate steps that can be checked
  • Compare independent sampling with search over a step tree
  • Explain the role of a verifier and what happens when it is unreliable
  • Estimate the accuracy/cost frontier of a reasoning strategy

Concept An operational definition of reasoning

“Does it reason?” is a question about an unobservable process. The useful version is operational: reasoning is the production of intermediate steps that a criterion can evaluate. That definition is testable, and it is the one used throughout this module.

Under it, three things become measurable: whether a step follows from its predecessors, whether the final answer is right, and how much computation was spent to get there. Every claim in the rest of the module is a statement about one of those three.

Concept Why more tokens can mean more thinking

A decoder performs a fixed amount of computation per generated token. A hard problem that cannot be solved in one pass can sometimes be solved by writing intermediate results: each token is another pass through the network, conditioned on everything written so far. This is the mechanism behind inference-time compute scaling, and it explains why a shorter trace on the same model is not equivalent to a longer one.

It also sets the cost model. More steps means more tokens, which means more time and memory. Extra computation is a trade, not a free improvement.

Concept Search over a step tree

Once steps are explicit, a solution is a path through a tree of partial states. Three strategies cover most practice:

  • Greedy — expand the single best-scoring node. Cheapest; cannot recover from a locally attractive mistake.
  • *Beam search* — keep the best $b$ partial solutions alive. Marginally more expensive per step, much more robust to a misleading first step.
  • Best-of-n sampling — draw complete candidate paths independently and pick the best by verifier score. Simple to parallelise, but its accuracy depends on how often the sampling distribution produces a correct path at all.

The verifier is the bottleneck

Search optimises the objective it is given. A verifier that rewards confident wrong steps steers search toward wrong answers with high confidence — scaling the search makes the failure more reliable, not less. “Verification” is a promise about a checker, not about truth.

Concept Verification in practice

Verifiable rewards come from checkers: a unit test, a solver, a formal proof assistant, a database query whose result can be compared with the expected answer. Where a checker exists, reinforcement learning on it is well-posed. Where it does not, the reward must come from a learned model, and the reward-model caveats from Module 4 return in full.

The lesson in the numbers

Greedy spends the fewest calls and commits to the branch that looks best at step one — which, on this tree, is wrong. A wider beam spends more calls and finds the correct path. Best-of-n depends on how well the sampling distribution covers the correct branch; set the temperature very low and it degenerates toward greedy.

Outcome rewards versus verifiable rewards

The same tree scored with a step verifier versus only the final answer.

  • step verifier Scores every partial solution, so search can prune early. Cost: a reliable step-level scorer, which is itself a trained model or a human process.
  • outcome only Scores only terminals. Cheap and unambiguous, but the search must finish a path to learn anything, and credit assignment across steps is unresolved.
  • miscalibrated verifier A scorer that rewards confident wrong steps is worse than no scorer: search optimises it faithfully and finds the wrong answer more reliably.

Worked example

Reading the numbers from the lab

On the course’s tree, greedy selects b2 at a verifier score of 0.90 but it is the wrong answer, spending 5 verifier calls. A beam of three selects c3 (score 0.97, correct) for 9 calls. Best-of-six sampling selects c3 with 17 calls.

The beam’s extra calls bought the correct answer here. That will not always be true: on a tree where the highest-scoring terminal is also correct, greedy is both cheapest and right. The point is that the trade-off is a property of the score landscape, not a universal rule.

The ideas

  • More generated tokens mean more sequential computation, which is why chains help.
  • Generating several paths and selecting with a verifier is search with a learned heuristic.
  • Without verification, extra samples only amplify the model prior.

Practice

Q. What operational definition of reasoning does this course use? — concept

  • ✓ Producing intermediate steps that can be checked against a task criterion
  • Responding faster than a baseline model
  • Using more parameters than a baseline model
  • Storing more facts in the parameters

Why: Reasoning is treated operationally: intermediate steps plus a way to verify or score them. This makes claims testable instead of philosophical.

Q. On the course’s toy reasoning tree, greedy search spends the fewest verifier calls. What does comparing it with beam search show? — concept

  • ✓ More verification calls can buy correctness when step scores are locally misleading
  • Greedy search is always wrong
  • Beam search is always cheaper
  • Verification calls are free

Why: Greedy follows the highest immediate score and ends on the wrong terminal; the wider beam spends more calls and finds the correct path. The trade-off is real, not free.

Q. A verifier is systematically overconfident about a wrong family of answers. What is the expected effect of scaling search? — concept

  • ✓ It amplifies the verifier’s bias, selecting wrong answers more reliably
  • It removes the bias through averaging
  • It has no effect because the model is frozen
  • It converts the task into a retrieval problem

Why: Search optimises the combination of model proposals and verifier scores. A biased verifier is optimised just as faithfully as an accurate one.

Q. A reasoning system samples many candidate answers and a learned verifier picks one, and the system is confidently wrong. What is the most likely cause, and what would you check? — transfer

  • ✓ The verifier is the weak half: the search is adversarial to it, so it finds the candidate the verifier is most wrong about. Check the verifier against answers it was not trained on
  • The proposer is too weak, because the correct answer was never sampled
  • The sampling is too random, because the temperature was set too low
  • The prompt is too long, because the context is truncated

Why: The search is an adversary. It looks for the candidate that maximises the verifier’s score, which is not the same as the best candidate. A verifier that is right most of the time on the candidates it was trained on can be fooled by the ones the search produces. That is why the two halves have to be strong together, and why the pair is usually weaker than either half alone.

Go and do it

Run greedy, best-of-n and beam search over an explicit step tree with verifier scores, and compare correctness against verifier calls. Open Search a reasoning tree in the llm-foundations-lab application.

Lesson 17. Learning to reason

Supervised traces, process supervision and RL

Estimated study time: 30 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe how reasoning traces are collected and filtered
  • Contrast outcome supervision with process supervision
  • Explain the credit-assignment problem for intermediate steps
  • Motivate on-policy distillation and scaling training for reasoning

The ideas

  • Outcome rewards tell you the final answer was right, not which step earned it.
  • Process supervision provides a reward at every step, at the cost of annotation and reward hacking risk.
  • On-policy distillation learns from correct traces the model itself can produce.

Practice

Q. Which statement about process supervision is correct? — concept

  • ✓ It rewards intermediate steps, which helps credit assignment but costs step-level annotation and can be gamed
  • It rewards only the final answer
  • It eliminates the need for a verifier
  • It cannot be combined with reinforcement learning

Why: Step-level rewards localise credit, at the price of obtaining reliable step labels — the classic trade-off against outcome-only rewards.

Q. Why does outcome-only supervision make credit assignment hard? — concept

  • ✓ A single final reward must be attributed across many intermediate steps, and one bad step may be invisible
  • Because the final answer is unknown during training
  • Because the model has no output layer
  • Because tokenisation loses step boundaries

Why: One scalar at the end gives no information about which step was responsible, especially when a wrong step still happens to produce a correct answer.

Q. A team can afford process labels for one trace in ten, and outcome labels for all of them. What should it label with what, and why? — transfer

  • ✓ Process-label the tenth, because the outcome labels already give the cheap signal and only the process labels can tell a right answer reached by a wrong route from one reached by a right one
  • Outcome-label the tenth and process-label the rest, because process labels are more informative per label
  • Label everything with outcome labels; process labels are not worth their cost
  • Label everything with process labels, because outcome labels are misleading

Why: Outcome labels are cheap and give the broad signal; process labels are expensive and give the specific one. The combination that pays is to spend the expensive labels on a sample in order to learn what a good step looks like, and then use that to check the cheap ones. Process supervision does not make outcome labels wrong — it makes them blind.

Go and do it

Train a toy step scorer on outcome-only and process labels and compare the credit it assigns to each step. Open Outcome vs. step rewards in the llm-foundations-lab application.

  • §6.4.4 Scaling Training for Reasoning · p. 268 — Scale and data considerations in reasoning training.

  • On-policy distillation — Learn from correct traces the model itself generates
  • Verifiable-reward training — Rewards computed by a checker

Lesson 18. Evaluating reasoning, honestly

Metrics, benchmarks and open questions

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Choose an evaluation protocol that matches the claimed capability
  • Contrast outcome-based and process-based evaluation
  • Explain contamination and the difference between memorisation and reasoning
  • List the open questions the source itself leaves unresolved

The ideas

  • A metric measures a task setup, not an abstract capability.
  • Held-out, contamination-checked evaluation is a design constraint, not an afterthought.
  • Whether models genuinely reason remains contested; the honest answer is that the evidence is mixed.

Practice

Q. A benchmark reports 82% accuracy, but 30% of its items appeared in the model’s pre-training data. What is the correct interpretation? — concept

  • ✓ The score is inflated by contamination and may reflect memorisation rather than the claimed capability
  • The score is still valid because the metric is defined correctly
  • The score is understated
  • Contamination only matters for vision benchmarks

Why: A metric measures a task setup. If the setup leaks training items, the measurement no longer supports the capability claim.

Q. Which evaluation design best supports a claim that a method improves reasoning? — concept

  • ✓ Held-out, contamination-checked tasks with a matched compute budget and an error analysis of the traces
  • A single benchmark run with the highest temperature
  • Reporting only the best of ten runs
  • Reporting the metric without the protocol

Why: Matching compute makes the comparison about method rather than budget, and held-out contamination-checked tasks keep the claim about capability rather than recall.

Q. A benchmark is published on the web, and a model is evaluated on it two years later. What has to be reported for the number to mean anything? — transfer

  • ✓ The contamination rate and the item-level breakdown, because a model that has seen the answers scores higher for reasons that have nothing to do with reasoning
  • The overall score and the model size, because the score is the score
  • The training data size, because a bigger model is better
  • Nothing extra, because the benchmark is the benchmark

Why: Anything published publicly before the evaluation is very likely in the pre-training or fine-tuning data. The number therefore measures a mixture of capability and recognition, and the two can only be separated by reporting how much of the benchmark was in the training data and how the model did item by item.

Go and do it

Score the same synthetic results under outcome-only, process-aware and cost-adjusted protocols and see how the conclusion changes. Open Protocol comparison in the llm-foundations-lab application.

Appendix A — Glossary

Pre-training — Training a general model before any task is specified

Optimising a model on a broad objective over large unlabelled corpora so that its parameters transfer to many downstream tasks. In the book’s unified notation the model o = g(x₀…xₘ; θ) is first fitted on the general objective, then adapted.

Self-supervision — Supervision constructed from the data itself

Building training targets by hiding or shifting parts of the input, so that no human annotation is needed. Masked-token prediction and next-token prediction are the two canonical instances.

Foundation model — A pre-trained model adapted to many tasks

A large pre-trained model that serves as a starting point for fine-tuning or prompting across many tasks, rather than being built for one task.

Fine-tuning — Continuing training on task or instruction data

Updating the parameters of a pre-trained model on a smaller, targeted dataset (labelled examples or instructions) so that it specialises.

Autoregressive — Each token conditioned on the ones before it

A factorisation of a sequence distribution into per-token conditionals: Pr(x) = ∏ᵢ Pr(xᵢ | x₀…xᵢ₋₁). This is the objective of decoder-only language models and the loop followed at generation time.

Language model — A distribution over token sequences

A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens, or equivalently predicts the distribution of the next token given a context.

Masked language model — Predict hidden tokens from both sides

An encoder-only pre-training objective: replace a fraction of tokens with [MASK] (or a random token, or nothing), then predict the originals using the full surrounding context. Because inference at generation time never sees [MASK], the objective suits representation learning rather than open-ended generation.

Span corruption — Delete spans; ask the decoder to restore them

An encoder–decoder pre-training objective that removes contiguous spans from the input and trains the decoder to regenerate them, producing a sequence-to-sequence reconstruction task.

Classification head — A small output layer added for a task

A task-specific layer attached to a pre-trained encoder (often a softmax over pooled or [CLS] representations) and trained on labelled data.

Token — The unit a model reads and predicts

The atomic unit of text in a model’s vocabulary. Tokens may be whole words, subword pieces, characters or bytes; every sequence the model processes is a sequence of token ids.

Token embedding — A learned vector for a token id

A lookup table mapping each vocabulary item to a dense vector of dimension d. In this course the table is a deterministic toy table so that learners can inspect the numbers.

Positional encoding — Information about where a token sits

A vector added to the token embedding so the model can use order, since attention itself is permutation-invariant. Sinusoidal encodings use sin/cos at geometrically spaced frequencies; learned and rotary variants also exist.

Query, key, value (Q, K, V) — Three projections of the hidden states

Q, K and V are linear projections of the same hidden matrix H: Q = H W_q, K = H W_k, V = H W_v. Queries are compared with keys to produce attention weights, which are then applied to values.

Scaled dot-product attention — Softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V

The core attention operation. The 1/√d scaling keeps logits in a range where the softmax has usable gradients as the head dimension grows.

Causal mask — Block attention to future positions

An additive matrix M with M(i,k) = 0 for i ≥ k and M(i,k) = −∞ otherwise, added to the scaled scores before the softmax. It makes the model autoregressive: position i can only see positions 0…i.

Softmax — Turn scores into a probability distribution

A normalising function that exponentiates scores and divides by their sum. Implementations subtract the maximum for numerical stability; the result is unchanged.

Logits — Unnormalised scores before softmax

The raw real-valued outputs of the final projection. Their softmax is the model’s token distribution; decoding algorithms operate on logits before or after this normalisation.

Scaling law — Predictable power-law loss trends

An empirical regularity: loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size and compute, which allows training runs to be planned before they are executed.

Compute-optimal scaling — Balance parameters and tokens for a budget

The finding that, for a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should be increased together in a balanced ratio rather than scaling only one of them.

Data parallelism — Replicate the model, split the batch

Each device holds a copy of the parameters and processes a different batch slice; gradients are synchronised across devices. Memory per device stays high because every replica holds the whole model.

Tensor parallelism — Split a layer across devices

Individual weight matrices are partitioned across devices and partial results are combined with communication, which reduces per-device memory at the cost of frequent collective operations.

KV cache — Stored keys and values for past tokens

Autoregressive decoding needs the keys and values of every previous position. Storing them turns repeated recomputation into a memory read. The footprint is 2·L·h_kv·d_h·T·bytes per sequence.

Grouped-query attention — Fewer KV heads than query heads

Several query heads share one key/value head, reducing the cache by the ratio h_kv/h_q while retaining more expressiveness than multi-query attention (a single shared head).

Context window — How many tokens the model can condition on

The maximum number of tokens available in one forward pass. Prompts, retrieved passages, examples and generated tokens all consume this budget.

Position interpolation — Stretching a model beyond its trained length

Techniques that rescale or adjust positional information so that a model trained on shorter sequences can process longer contexts with acceptable quality.

Prompt — The text that conditions a frozen model

The input context given to a model at inference time: instructions, data, demonstrations and an output contract. Prompting changes conditioning, not parameters.

In-context learning — Learning a pattern from examples inside the prompt

The ability to infer a task from demonstrations in the context window, without parameter updates. It is conditioning: the demonstrations bias the next-token distribution.

Zero-shot prompting — Task description with no examples

A prompt that specifies the task in words without worked examples.

Few-shot prompting — A handful of demonstrations in the prompt

A prompt that includes several input→output examples before the real query. Examples cost context budget and can introduce their own biases.

Chain of thought — Write the intermediate steps

Prompting a model to produce reasoning steps before its answer. Because each token is a sequential computation step, longer traces let the model compute more before committing.

Problem decomposition — Split one hard task into easier sub-tasks

Rewriting a task as a sequence of sub-problems, each simple enough to be solved and checked individually.

Self-refinement — Revise a candidate answer

Producing a draft and then criticising or revising it. It only reliably helps when an external check supplies new information.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — Retrieve passages, then generate

A pipeline that selects relevant documents with a retriever and places them in the prompt so the generator conditions on up-to-date or private information.

Cosine similarity — Angle between two vectors

The dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their norms. Values near 1 mean aligned directions, which is how a retriever ranks passages against a query.

Tool use — The model emits a structured action

The model produces a call to an external function or API in a defined format; the result is returned to the context. Correctness depends on the contract, not only on fluent text.

Soft prompt — Learned continuous prompt vectors

Optimised input embeddings prepended to the input instead of discrete text. They are parameters, trained with gradients, and cannot be read as natural language.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) — Imitate demonstrated responses

Fine-tuning on instruction/response pairs with the cross-entropy loss applied to response tokens, teaching the format and style of useful answers.

Instruction tuning — Fine-tuning to follow instructions

Supervised fine-tuning with instruction-formatted data, which turns a text continuation model into one that responds to requests.

Cross-entropy loss — Negative log-likelihood of the target

For a target distribution p and prediction q, H(p,q) = −Σ p log q. With a one-hot target it reduces to the negative log-probability of the correct class or token.

RLHF — Reinforcement learning from human feedback

A pipeline that trains a reward model on human comparisons, then optimises the policy to score well under that reward while staying close to a reference model.

Reward model — A scalar scorer trained on comparisons

A model r(x, y) that assigns a scalar quality score to a response. It is trained on pairwise preferences and then used as the objective for policy optimisation.

Bradley–Terry model — Preference as a sigmoid of score differences

A model of pairwise comparison where the probability that a beats b is the logistic function of the difference of their scores.

KL divergence — How far one distribution is from another

D_KL(p‖q) = Σ p log(p/q) ≥ 0, equal to zero only when the distributions match. It appears in RLHF as a penalty keeping the tuned policy close to its reference.

PPO — The policy-gradient algorithm used in RLHF

Proximal policy optimisation: a policy-gradient method that limits how far each update moves the policy, requiring both a policy and a value function.

DPO (direct preference optimisation) — Preference learning without an explicit reward model

Substituting the closed-form optimal policy into the Bradley–Terry likelihood yields a loss over policy/reference log-ratios, so preferences are optimised directly.

Reference model — The frozen model a policy is compared against

A copy of the model before preference tuning. Its log-probabilities appear in the DPO ratio and in the RLHF KL penalty, and it is never updated.

Log-ratio — log(π/π_ref) between policy and reference

The quantity log Pr_θ(y|x) − log Pr_ref(y|x). Under the DPO derivation it equals the reward divided by β, up to a prompt-dependent constant.

Prefill — Process the prompt in parallel

The first inference phase, in which all prompt positions are processed simultaneously and their keys and values are written into the cache.

Decode — Generate one token at a time

The second inference phase: each step computes one query, attends to cached keys and values, and appends a new token.

Prefix caching — Reuse a shared prompt’s cached state

Storing the KV state of a common prefix (a system prompt, for example) so that later requests skip its prefill computation.

Continuous batching — Admit and retire requests every step

Scheduling that adds new requests to a running batch as soon as slots free up, rather than waiting for a fixed batch to finish, which raises utilisation.

Temperature (τ) — Rescale logits before softmax

Dividing logits by τ before the softmax. τ < 1 sharpens the distribution (less randomness), τ > 1 flattens it (more). τ must be positive; zero is the limit, approached with a small positive value.

Top-k sampling — Sample from the k most likely tokens

Keep the k highest-probability tokens, renormalise their mass and sample from that pool. A fixed pool size can be too small in flat distributions and too large in peaked ones.

Top-p (nucleus) sampling — Sample from the smallest set reaching mass p

Sort tokens by probability, add them until the cumulative mass reaches p, then renormalise and sample. The pool size adapts to how peaked the distribution is.

Greedy decoding — Always take the most likely token

A deterministic decoder that selects argmax at every step. It is reproducible and predictable but cannot explore alternatives.

Beam search — Keep the best b partial sequences

A search that expands several candidate sequences in parallel and keeps the highest-scoring b at each step. Without a length or score calibration it favours short, high-probability outputs.

Inference-time scaling — Buy accuracy with extra computation at run time

Spending additional tokens, samples or search steps during inference — context scaling, search scaling, output ensembling, thinking-path generation — instead of changing the model.

Throughput — Tokens served per unit time

Aggregate production rate across all concurrent requests, as opposed to latency for one request. Batching raises throughput while usually increasing per-request latency.

Reasoning — Checkable intermediate computation

In this course, reasoning is defined operationally: producing intermediate steps that a criterion — a test, a verifier, a formal check — can evaluate. This keeps claims empirically testable.

Test-time compute — Computation spent after training

Any inference-time expenditure — longer traces, multiple samples, search — that can improve accuracy without changing weights.

Verifier — A scorer that judges candidate solutions

A function or model that scores a candidate answer or step. Search and best-of-n are only as good as the verifier they optimise against.

Search strategy — How candidate reasoning paths are explored

The rule for expanding and pruning partial solutions: greedy, beam, best-of-n, tree search. Each trades verifier calls against the risk of missing a correct path.

Process supervision — Reward every step, not only the answer

Training with step-level feedback, which localises credit assignment but requires reliable step labels and can be exploited by the policy.

Process reward model (PRM) — A scorer for intermediate steps

A reward model trained to score partial solutions, used to guide search or as a reward signal during training.

Credit assignment — Which step deserves the reward?

The problem of attributing a final outcome to the intermediate decisions that produced it — the central difficulty of outcome-only supervision.

On-policy distillation — Learn from correct traces the model itself generates

Training on reasoning traces sampled from the current model and filtered for correctness, which keeps the training distribution close to the inference distribution.

Verifiable-reward training — Rewards computed by a checker

Reinforcement learning where the reward comes from an automatic checker (a unit test, a solver, a proof checker) rather than a learned preference model.

Benchmark — A task suite used for evaluation

A fixed set of tasks with a scoring protocol. Benchmarks measure performance under a setup; they do not directly measure an abstract capability.

Contamination — Test data seen during training

Overlap between evaluation items and training data, which inflates scores and can convert a reasoning measurement into a recall measurement.

pass@k — Solve at least one of k attempts

A metric that counts a task as solved if any of k sampled attempts is correct. It measures coverage under a sampling budget, and should be reported with that budget.

Outcome-based evaluation — Judge the final answer only

Scoring a solution by its final answer. Cheap to automate and reproducible, but blind to whether the reasoning was sound or accidentally correct.

1. Tokenisation

The first decision, and the one everything else is priced against

A tokeniser decides what a token is, and therefore how long your corpus is, how big your embedding table is, and how many tokens of compute your training run costs. This module builds a byte-pair encoding from scratch and measures the trade-off it sets up.

Learning outcomes

  • Train a byte-pair encoding and explain the merge rule
  • Compute the bytes-per-token ratio and say what it decides
  • Explain why the vocabulary size and the sequence length trade against each other

Lesson 1. The tokeniser

Learning to merge bytes into words

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the byte-pair encoding rule and run it by hand on a short example
  • Explain why the encoding starts from bytes rather than characters
  • Compute the bytes-per-token ratio of a corpus

The ideas

  • The tokeniser is trained, not designed: the merges are whatever the corpus supports.
  • Starting from bytes means the vocabulary can represent any text, at the price of a long sequence.
  • The bytes-per-token ratio is the number that decides your training bill.

Practice

*Q. What does a byte-pair encoding start from? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The 256 bytes of the text
  • A fixed list of words
  • The most frequent words in the corpus
  • Unicode code points

Correct, which is why it can represent any text.

Why: Starting from the bytes means the tokeniser can represent any text at all, and the merges it learns are whatever the corpus supports.

*Q. A corpus is 8,000,000 bytes of text and the tokeniser produces 2,000,000 tokens. How many bytes per token is that? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 4 bytes per token

Why: Exactly 4 bytes per token. The ratio is the number that decides the training bill: a corpus of B bytes becomes B ÷ 4 tokens, and the compute follows the token count.

Go and do it

Train a byte-pair encoding on a generated corpus and watch the merges accumulate. Open Watch the merges happen in the lm-from-scratch application.

Where this came from

  • §1 Overview and tokenization · p. 1 — The tokenisation approach the assignment builds on, and the reason the vocabulary size and the sequence length trade against each other.
  • §assignment1 Assignment 1 — Basics · p. 1 — The tokeniser, the model and the optimiser the assignment asks you to build.

The words this lesson uses

  • Tokeniser — The program that turns text into a sequence of integers.
  • Byte-pair encoding — A tokeniser learned by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair.
  • Vocabulary — The set of tokens the tokeniser can produce.
  • Bytes per token — How many characters of text one token stands for.

Lesson 2. The vocabulary economy

Every token you save is a parameter you do not have

Estimated study time: 18 minutes

What you will learn

  • Explain the trade between the vocabulary size and the sequence length
  • Compute the embedding parameters a vocabulary implies
  • Argue for a particular vocabulary size on cost grounds

The ideas

  • A larger vocabulary means a longer sequence for the same text, and more parameters in the embedding.
  • The cost of a vocabulary is paid twice: in parameters, and in tokens.
  • The optimum depends on the model width, which is why the two cannot be chosen separately.

Practice

*Q. Why does a larger vocabulary not simply make training cheaper? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ Because the embedding and output matrices get larger
  • Because the sequences get longer, so the attention cost grows
  • Because the optimiser has more states to carry
  • It does make training cheaper

Correct — that is half of it.

Why: A larger vocabulary shortens the sequence but enlarges the two vocabulary-sized matrices. The two effects pull in opposite directions, which is why the vocabulary and the width have to be chosen together.

*Q. A model with d_model = 512 uses a vocabulary of 100,000 tokens. How many parameters do the token embeddings alone require, in millions? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 51.2 ± 0.01

Why: The embedding matrix is vocabulary × d_model: 100,000 × 512 = 51.2 million parameters before a single layer is built. Every token saved from the vocabulary is a parameter that can be spent elsewhere — which is why the vocabulary size is an economic decision, not a natural constant.

Go and do it

Watch the embedding parameters and the corpus length move against each other. Open The cost of a vocabulary in the lm-from-scratch application.

Where this came from

  • §1 Overview and tokenization · p. 1 — The argument that the vocabulary size and the model dimensions have to be chosen together.

The words this lesson uses

  • Vocabulary — The set of tokens the tokeniser can produce.
  • Embedding — The matrix that maps a token id to a vector.
  • Context length — The maximum number of tokens the model attends over at once.

Read first: The tokeniser

2. The Architecture

A stack of matrices, and the shapes that go with them

The decoder-only transformer is a small number of matrices. This module writes them down, counts their parameters, and shows which of them dominate the bill.

Learning outcomes

  • Write the decoder block: the attention, the feed-forward, and the residual connections
  • Count the parameters of a model and say which part dominates
  • Explain what tying the output projection to the embedding does

Lesson 3. The decoder block

Attention, a feed-forward layer, and two residual connections

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the decoder block and name every tensor in it
  • Explain the pre-norm ordering and what it buys
  • Explain why the feed-forward block is usually wider than the residual stream

The ideas

  • A block is a residual connection around an attention, and another around a feed-forward.
  • The feed-forward block is where most of the parameters live.
  • The pre-norm ordering keeps the residual stream clean, which is what makes deep stacks trainable.

Practice

*Q. Which part of a decoder block usually holds the most parameters? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The feed-forward block
  • The attention projections
  • The layer norms
  • The residual connections

Correct: two matrices of width × dFf each.

Why: The feed-forward block has a width × dFf matrix and a dFf × width matrix, and with dFf usually several times the width it dominates the block.

*Q. A pre-norm block normalises its input before the sub-layer rather than after it. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. Normalising first keeps the residual stream unscaled, which is what makes a deep stack of blocks trainable without careful initialisation.

Go and do it

Count every parameter of a model and see which part of it dominates. Open Count the parameters in the lm-from-scratch application.

Where this came from

  • §3 Architectures and hyperparameters · p. 1 — The architecture the assignment builds, and the hyperparameter choices it makes.

The words this lesson uses

  • Transformer — The stack of attention and feed-forward blocks that makes a language model.
  • Attention — The part of the block that lets each position look at the others.
  • Feed-forward block — A two-layer network applied to each position independently.
  • Residual connection — Adding a block’s input to its output.
  • RMSNorm — Normalising a vector by its root-mean-square, then scaling it.

Read first: The vocabulary economy

Lesson 4. The parameter budget

Which matrices are large, and why

Estimated study time: 18 minutes

What you will learn

  • Break a model’s parameters into their components
  • Explain when the embedding dominates the parameter count
  • Explain what tying the output projection does

The ideas

  • The embedding and the output projection are the only vocabulary-sized matrices.
  • Tying them halves the largest single block of parameters, at the cost of some capability.
  • Everything else scales with the width and the depth, not the vocabulary.

Practice

*Q. A model has a vocabulary of 32,000, a width of 768 and 12 layers, and it ties its output projection to the embedding. How many parameters does the embedding account for, in millions? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 24.576 ± 0.001 million parameters

Why: 32,000 × 768 = 24,576,000, which is 24.576 million. With the output tied, the vocabulary-sized parameters are paid for once instead of twice.

*Q. What does tying the output projection to the input embedding do to the parameter budget? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • It halves the embedding matrix
  • ✓ It removes a separate vocabulary × d_model output matrix, whose cost grows with the vocabulary
  • It makes the model train faster without changing the count
  • It removes the positional encoding

Correct — the same matrix reads the logits out.

Why: The output projection is another vocabulary × d_model matrix — at large vocabularies it rivals the embedding itself. Tying shares one matrix for both roles, and for small models the embedding can dominate the entire parameter count, which is exactly when the tie matters most.

Go and do it

The parameter breakdown as the width, the depth and the vocabulary move. Open The budget in the lm-from-scratch application.

Where this came from

  • §3 Architectures and hyperparameters · p. 1 — The model dimensions and how they are chosen.

The words this lesson uses

  • Parameter count — How many numbers the model has.
  • Weight tying — Using the token embedding as the output projection.

3. Resource Accounting

How much arithmetic, and how much memory, and which one binds

Before you train anything, you can work out what it will cost. This module counts the floating-point operations of a training step, the memory it needs, and the arithmetic intensity that decides whether the arithmetic units or the memory bandwidth is the bottleneck.

Learning outcomes

  • Count the FLOPs of a forward pass and of a training step
  • Compute the memory a training step needs, in all four of its components
  • Compute the arithmetic intensity and place it against the machine’s balance point
  • Explain why the attention kernel is memory bound even when the step is not

Lesson 5. The FLOPs

What a training step costs before you run it

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Count the FLOPs of a forward pass from the matrix shapes alone
  • Explain why a training step is about three forward passes
  • Predict how the cost changes with the width, the depth and the sequence length

The ideas

  • A matrix–matrix multiply of an m × k by a k × n costs 2mnk floating-point operations.
  • The backward pass costs about twice the forward pass, so a step is about three forwards.
  • The cost of a run is the cost of a step times the number of steps, and nothing is a surprise.

Practice

*Q. A matrix–matrix multiply of an m × k by a k × n matrix costs how many floating-point operations? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 2

Why: Exactly 2mnk. There are mn outputs, each needing k multiplications and k additions, and the additions are counted as a second operation.

*Q. Why is a training step about three forward passes? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The backward pass costs about twice the forward pass
  • The optimiser needs a second pass to check the update
  • The activations are recomputed
  • The data is loaded twice

Correct.

Why: The backward pass computes the gradient with respect to the inputs and the gradient with respect to the weights, and the second of those costs about as much as the forward pass itself.

Go and do it

Break a training step into its terms and watch them move with the shape. Open Count the arithmetic in the lm-from-scratch application.

Where this came from

  • §2 PyTorch and resource accounting · p. 1 — The FLOP accounting, and the rule that a matrix–matrix multiply costs 2mnk.

The words this lesson uses

  • FLOPs — Floating-point operations.
  • Training step — One batch, one forward pass, one backward pass, one update.
  • Arithmetic intensity — Floating-point operations per byte of memory traffic.

Read first: The decoder block

Lesson 6. The memory hierarchy

The wall your arithmetic runs into

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute the memory a training step needs, in all four of its components
  • Compute the arithmetic intensity and compare it with the machine’s balance point
  • Explain why the attention kernel is memory bound even when the whole step is not

The ideas

  • Four things have to fit: the parameters, the gradients, the optimiser state and the activations.
  • Arithmetic intensity is the number of operations per byte, and it decides what the bottleneck is.
  • The attention kernel’s intensity is fixed by the head dimension, which is why it has to be tiled.

Practice

*Q. What is the arithmetic intensity of a kernel? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Floating-point operations per byte of memory traffic
  • Bytes of memory per floating-point operation
  • The fraction of the peak rate the kernel reaches
  • The number of arithmetic units the kernel uses

Correct.

Why: Intensity is operations per byte. Compare it with the machine’s balance point — the intensity at which the two ceilings meet — and you know which of them binds.

*Q. Why is the attention kernel memory bound even when the whole training step is not? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ Its intensity is fixed by the head dimension, which is small
  • It runs on a slower processor
  • It reads more data than the other kernels
  • It uses more arithmetic units

Correct.

Why: The attention kernel does about dModel of arithmetic per byte it moves, which is below the balance point of a modern accelerator. That is why it has to be tiled, and why FlashAttention is a memory-layout problem as much as an arithmetic one.

Go and do it

Place the workload on the roofline and see which constraint binds. Open The roofline in the lm-from-scratch application.

  • §2 PyTorch and resource accounting · p. 2 — The memory hierarchy, the arithmetic intensity, and the roofline.
  • §5 GPUs, TPUs and the memory hierarchy · p. 1 — The hardware the arithmetic has to fit into, and the balance point of a real accelerator.

The words this lesson uses

  • Arithmetic intensity — Floating-point operations per byte of memory traffic.
  • Roofline — The ceiling on a kernel’s attainable rate.
  • Balance point — The intensity at which a machine’s two ceilings meet.
  • Activation memory — The intermediate values kept so the backward pass can use them.

4. Systems and Parallelism

What it costs to spread a model across machines

A model that does not fit on one device has to be split. This module covers the three kinds of parallelism and, for each of them, the communication that has to happen and the arithmetic it buys.

Learning outcomes

  • Name the three kinds of parallelism and what each one splits
  • Compute the communication a data-parallel step needs
  • Compute the ratio of communication to computation, and say when it stops paying

Lesson 7. Parallelism

Three ways to split a model, and what each one costs

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Name data, tensor and pipeline parallelism and what each splits
  • Compute the communication a data-parallel step needs
  • Compute the ratio of communication to computation, and say when it stops paying

The ideas

  • Data parallelism splits the batch and adds a gradient all-reduce per step.
  • Tensor parallelism splits a single matrix and adds an all-reduce per layer.
  • Pipeline parallelism splits the layers and adds a point-to-point send per stage.
  • The split is worth it when the communication is smaller than the arithmetic it saves.

Practice

*Q. What does data parallelism split? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The batch
  • The layers
  • The individual matrices
  • The vocabulary

Correct.

Why: Data parallelism gives every device the same model and a different slice of the batch, then all-reduces the gradients before the update.

*Q. Data parallelism is worth it when the gradient all-reduce costs less than the arithmetic it saves. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. The all-reduce touches every parameter, and the saving from a larger batch is the difference in the number of steps. Past some size the communication wins.

Go and do it

  • §assignment2 Assignment 2 — Systems · p. 1 — The systems assignment: profiling, a memory-efficient kernel, and a distributed run.

The words this lesson uses

  • Data parallelism — Splitting the batch across devices and averaging the gradients.
  • Tensor parallelism — Splitting a single matrix across devices.
  • Pipeline parallelism — Splitting the layers across devices and moving the activations along.
  • All-reduce — Summing a tensor across every device and giving the result to all of them.

5. Data

The part of the pipeline that decides what the model knows

The tokens are the training set, and how they are chosen is a research decision in its own right. This module covers the sources, the filtering, the deduplication, and what each stage is for.

Learning outcomes

  • Say what each stage of a data pipeline is for
  • Explain why deduplication changes the token count
  • Argue for the mixture being a decision rather than a default

Lesson 8. The data pipeline

From a crawl to a training set

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Name the stages of a language-modeling data pipeline and what each is for
  • Explain why deduplication changes the token count
  • Argue that the mixture is a decision rather than a default

The ideas

  • Every filtering stage removes tokens, and the stages are not independent.
  • Deduplication is not a tidy-up; it changes what the model learns.
  • The mixture over sources is a research decision, and it should be argued for.

Practice

*Q. What is the mixture in a data pipeline? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The proportions in which the sources are combined
  • The list of filters applied to the corpus
  • The order the documents are shuffled in
  • The tokeniser’s merge list

Correct.

Why: The mixture is a decision about what the model should know, and it deserves the same argument as any other hyperparameter.

*Q. Deduplication only tidies the corpus up; it does not change what the model learns. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: False

Why: No. Repeated text is a signal — the model learns differently when a document appears ten times — and removing it changes both the token count and the distribution.

6. Training and Evaluation

The loop, the loss, and what the number means

A training run is a loop over batches, and a language model is trained to predict the next token. This module runs a real one, in the browser, and reports what the loss and the perplexity actually measure.

Learning outcomes

  • Run a training loop and read the loss curve
  • Explain what the cross-entropy loss is measuring, token by token
  • Convert a loss into a perplexity and say what the conversion assumes
  • Say why a validation loss is a different measurement from a training loss

Lesson 9. The training loop

Batches, gradients, and the loss that falls

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the training loop and say what each step does
  • Explain the cross-entropy loss as a sum over tokens
  • Explain what the loss curve does and does not tell you

The ideas

  • A step is a batch, a forward pass, a backward pass and an update.
  • The loss is the average negative log-probability of the tokens that came next.
  • A falling loss is evidence the model is fitting; it is not evidence it generalises.

Practice

*Q. What does the cross-entropy loss measure for a language model? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The negative log-probability the model assigned to the token that actually came next
  • The error in the predicted token
  • The distance between the prediction and the label
  • The perplexity

Correct.

Why: Averaged over the tokens, the cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the corpus under the model, which is exactly what the model is trying to minimise.

*Q. A model reaches a cross-entropy of 2.3026. What is its perplexity? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 10

Why: e^2.3026 = 10, so exactly 10. A perplexity of 10 means the model was as uncertain about each token as a ten-way choice.

Train a real transformer in the browser and watch the loss fall. Open Run a training loop in the lm-from-scratch application.

The words this lesson uses

  • Cross-entropy — The average negative log-probability of the tokens that actually came next.
  • Batch — The set of sequences one step processes.
  • Gradient accumulation — Splitting a large batch into several small ones and adding the gradients.
  • Perplexity — The loss, exponentiated.

Lesson 10. The perplexity, and the number behind it

What the loss means when you exponentiate it

Estimated study time: 18 minutes

What you will learn

  • Convert a cross-entropy loss into a perplexity
  • State what the perplexity assumes about the distribution
  • Explain why the validation loss is a different measurement

The ideas

  • The perplexity is the loss, exponentiated: it is a number of effective choices.
  • It assumes the model is being scored against one fixed distribution.
  • A validation loss is a measurement; a training loss is a diagnostic.

Practice

*Q. Why is the validation loss a different measurement from the training loss? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It is computed on data the model never trained on
  • It is computed with a different tokeniser
  • It is the training loss, averaged
  • It uses a different loss function

Correct.

Why: The training loss is a diagnostic of the optimiser; the validation loss is a measurement of the model. The gap between them is the overfitting.

*Q. A model evaluates a document at a cross-entropy loss of 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity on that document? — numeric (warmup)***

Answer: 7.39 ± 0.02

Why: Perplexity is e^loss: e^2.0 ≈ 7.39. The number is the effective size of the fair coin the model is flipping per token — and it inherits every assumption the loss made about the distribution.

Lesson 11. Projecting the next run

What a power law lets you say before you spend the money

Estimated study time: 20 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the shape of the scaling laws and what they predict
  • Explain the compute-optimal allocation and the rule of thumb it gives
  • Say what a scaling law cannot tell you

The ideas

  • The loss falls as a power law in the compute, the data and the parameters.
  • For a fixed compute, there is an optimal size, and Chinchilla found where.
  • A scaling law is an extrapolation, and its uncertainty grows with the distance.

Practice

*Q. What does the IsoFLOP method find? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ The model size that minimises the loss for a fixed compute budget
  • The largest model the hardware can hold
  • The number of epochs before overfitting
  • The learning rate schedule

Correct.

Why: For each model size, find the data that uses the same compute, and read the best point off the curve. Chinchilla used it to find the compute-optimal allocation.

*Q. What can a scaling law tell you before any expensive run is spent? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • The exact loss the final model will reach
  • ✓ The shape of the loss curve, and therefore what the next budget is likely to buy
  • Whether the model will generalise to a new language
  • The optimal architecture

Correct — that is what the law is for, and also where it stops.

Why: A power law lets you say what the next doubling buys while it is still cheap to measure the curve. What it cannot tell you is what capabilities the scaling will produce — the shape of a loss is not a map of what the model learns.

Go and do it

Trace the compute-optimal frontier and read the optimal allocation off it. Open The IsoFLOP picture in the lm-from-scratch application.

  • IsoFLOP — Holding the compute fixed and sweeping the model size.

Appendix A — Glossary

Tokeniser — The program that turns text into a sequence of integers.

It defines what a token is. Everything downstream — the sequence length, the embedding size, the compute — is priced against it.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Byte-pair encoding — A tokeniser learned by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair.

It starts from the 256 bytes, so it can represent any text, and it learns its merges from the corpus. The merges are the model, not a design decision.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Vocabulary — The set of tokens the tokeniser can produce.

Its size sets the width of the embedding matrix and of the output projection, and it trades against how long the sequences become.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Bytes per token — How many characters of text one token stands for.

The ratio that decides your bill: a corpus of B bytes becomes B ÷ (bytes per token) tokens, and the training cost follows the token count.

Example: A corpus of 10 GB with 4 bytes per token — how many tokens? → About 2.5 billion tokens.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Embedding — The matrix that maps a token id to a vector.

Its shape is vocabulary × width, which makes it one of the two largest matrices in the model.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Context length — The maximum number of tokens the model attends over at once.

It sets the size of the positional embedding and, quadratically, the cost of the attention scores.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Transformer — The stack of attention and feed-forward blocks that makes a language model.

A decoder-only transformer is a residual stream with an attention block and a feed-forward block wrapped around each step.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Attention — The part of the block that lets each position look at the others.

Each position forms a query, compares it with every key, and mixes the values in proportion to the resulting scores.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Feed-forward block — A two-layer network applied to each position independently.

It holds most of the model’s parameters, which is why widening it is the usual way to add capacity.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Residual connection — Adding a block’s input to its output.

It gives the gradient a direct path, which is what makes a deep stack of blocks trainable at all.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

RMSNorm — Normalising a vector by its root-mean-square, then scaling it.

A simplification of LayerNorm with no mean subtraction and no bias. The gradient has a term from the mean that is easy to forget.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Parameter count — How many numbers the model has.

It decides the memory for the parameters, the gradients and the optimiser state — four bytes per parameter for the last two and two for the first.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Weight tying — Using the token embedding as the output projection.

It removes one vocabulary-sized matrix, which is often a large fraction of the parameters, at the cost of some expressiveness.

Course term

FLOPs — Floating-point operations.

A matrix–matrix multiply of an m × k by a k × n matrix costs 2mnk of them. That single rule is enough to cost a whole training run.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Training step — One batch, one forward pass, one backward pass, one update.

The backward pass costs about twice the forward, so a step is about three forwards.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Arithmetic intensity — Floating-point operations per byte of memory traffic.

It decides whether a kernel is limited by the arithmetic units or by the memory bandwidth, and it is the number the roofline is built on.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Balance point — The intensity at which a machine’s two ceilings meet.

A kernel above it is limited by memory; below it, by arithmetic. On a modern accelerator it is of order a hundred.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Roofline — The ceiling on a kernel’s attainable rate.

The smaller of the machine’s peak arithmetic rate and its bandwidth divided by the intensity. A kernel cannot beat the roof, and knowing which arm it is under tells you what to optimise.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Activation memory — The intermediate values kept so the backward pass can use them.

It scales with the sequence length and with the width, and it is usually the largest single term in the memory of a training step.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Data parallelism — Splitting the batch across devices and averaging the gradients.

Each device computes the same model on a different slice of the data, and the gradients are all-reduced before the update.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Tensor parallelism — Splitting a single matrix across devices.

It needs an all-reduce inside every layer, which is why it is usually confined to the fast interconnect inside a node.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Pipeline parallelism — Splitting the layers across devices and moving the activations along.

It needs a point-to-point send per stage, and it leaves the devices idle at the boundaries unless there are enough microbatches to fill the pipe.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

All-reduce — Summing a tensor across every device and giving the result to all of them.

Its cost is what decides whether data parallelism is worth it, and it is why the parameters have to be kept in a form the reduction can be applied to efficiently.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Corpus — The pile of text a model is trained on.

Its size in tokens is the training budget, and which text is in it is a research decision.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Deduplication — Removing text that appears more than once.

It is not a tidy-up. Repeated text is a signal, and removing it changes both the token count and what the model learns.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Filtering — Removing the documents a pipeline decides are not worth training on.

Each stage removes tokens, and the stages are not independent, so the order and the thresholds are decisions with consequences.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Mixture — The proportions in which the sources of a corpus are combined.

It is a decision about what the model should know, and it deserves the same argument as any other hyperparameter.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Cross-entropy — The average negative log-probability of the tokens that actually came next.

It is the objective of almost every language model, and it is the negative log-likelihood the model is trying to minimise.

Course term

Batch — The set of sequences one step processes.

It trades memory against the quality of the gradient: a bigger batch is a better estimate of the gradient and a larger activation footprint.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Gradient accumulation — Splitting a large batch into several small ones and adding the gradients.

It gives you the gradient of the large batch at the memory cost of the small one, at the cost of the activations of the small ones being alive at once.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Perplexity — The loss, exponentiated.

It is a number of effective choices: a perplexity of 10 means the model is as uncertain as a ten-way choice. It is only meaningful against a fixed tokenisation.

Example: A cross-entropy of 2.3 — what is the perplexity? → e^2.3 ≈ 10, so about ten effective choices per token.

Course term

Validation loss — The loss on data the model never trained on.

It is a measurement; the training loss is a diagnostic. The gap between them is the overfitting.

CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

Overfitting — The model learning the training data instead of the process behind it.

It shows up as a training loss that keeps falling while the validation loss does not.

Course term

Scaling law — A power law relating the loss to a resource.

The loss falls as a power law in the compute, the data and the parameters, with the exponent slowly improving.

Kaplan et al. (2020)

IsoFLOP — Holding the compute fixed and sweeping the model size.

The method that finds the compute-optimal allocation: for each model size, find the data that uses the same compute, and read the best point off the curve.

Hoffmann et al. (2022)

Compute-optimal — The allocation of parameters and data that minimises the loss for a fixed compute.

Chinchilla found that the parameters and the tokens should grow together, roughly twenty tokens per parameter — a rule of thumb, not a law.

Hoffmann et al. (2022)
