Appendix A — Glossary

Superposition — Several features packed into one direction of the model’s activation.

When a model has fewer dimensions than the features it represents, it cannot give each feature a direction of its own. It packs them together instead, and the features interfere.

Cunningham et al. (2023)

Interference — The cost two features pay for sharing a direction.

The cross term in the loss, (w_i·w_j)², weighted by the importance of the feature that pays it. It is zero for orthogonal directions and grows quadratically as they align.

Course term

Importance — How much a feature matters to the loss.

A weight on each feature’s squared error. The toy model assumes the importances follow a power law: a few features matter and a long tail does not.

Cunningham et al. (2023)

Polysemanticity — A neuron that responds to several unrelated things.

It is the direct consequence of superposition, and it is why you cannot read a model’s computation off its neurons.

Cunningham et al. (2023)

Monosemanticity — A direction that responds to one thing and nothing else.

The property a good dictionary feature has, and the one the interpretability scoring measures.

Cunningham et al. (2023)

Feature — A thing the model represents, as distinct from the neuron it uses.

A feature is a direction in activation space that corresponds to something the model can talk about. It need not be a neuron, and in a superposed model it usually is not.

Cunningham et al. (2023)

Dictionary feature — A feature found by a sparse autoencoder.

One element of the overcomplete dictionary the autoencoder learns. It is a candidate answer to "what is this model representing?".

Cunningham et al. (2023)

Sparse autoencoder — An autoencoder trained to reconstruct with a sparse code.

f = ReLU(W_enc(x − b_pre) + b_enc), x̂ = W_dec f + b_pre, with the loss ‖x − x̂‖² + λ‖f‖₁. The L1 term is what makes the code sparse, and the sparsity is what makes the features interpretable.

Cunningham et al. (2023)

L0 — The number of features that are active.

The count of non-zero entries in the code. It is the sparsity the penalty buys, and the smaller it is the more interpretable the dictionary tends to be.

Course term

Explained variance — How much of the activation the reconstruction accounts for.

One minus the reconstruction error, divided by the variance of the activations. A dictionary that explains the variance has not thrown the information away.

Course term

Activation patching — Run the model twice, and replace one activation in one of the runs.

If the output changes, the node that was patched was causally responsible for the change. It is the difference between "responds to" and "does".

Conmy et al. (2023)

Causal — A claim that survives an intervention.

A correlational claim holds over the data you have; a causal claim holds over the data you would have had if you had intervened.

Course term

Attribution — How much a component is responsible for the output.

The effect of patching it, measured against the largest effect any component could have had.

Conmy et al. (2023)

Circuit — A graph of components that accounts for a behaviour.

Not a list of the features a model uses, but a small set of components and the causal paths between them that together explain what the model did.

Conmy et al. (2023)

Node — A component of the graph that does one thing.

In a transformer the natural nodes are the attention heads and the feed-forward blocks, and the natural edges are the causal influences between them.

Elhage et al. (2021)

Path — A chain of causal influences from an input to the output.

What an explanation is made of: a small number of paths, each of which carries the signal that mattered.

Elhage et al. (2021)

Faithfulness — How much of the effect a proposed subgraph accounts for.

If a graph of nodes reproduces the output change when patched, it is faithful; the score is the fraction of the effect it explains.

Conmy et al. (2023)

Residual stream — The vector every component reads from and writes to.

The computational graph a transformer induces is a set of components reading from and writing to this one vector, and it is the graph that a circuit is a subgraph of.

Elhage et al. (2021)

Induction head — A head that completes a pattern it has already seen.

It matches the current token against the token that preceded each earlier position, attends to the position after the match, and copies that token. [A][B] … [A] becomes [A][B] … [A][B].

Olsson et al. (2022)

Previous-token head — A head whose attention is on the position before it.

It moves each token one position forward in the residual stream. The induction head reads that shifted content as its keys, which is the whole of the first head’s contribution.

Olsson et al. (2022)

Composition — One head’s output used as another head’s input.

Heads write to the residual stream, and a later head reads from it. A behaviour that neither head can produce alone can be produced by the two in composition — which is why an explanation has to talk about paths and not just heads.

Olsson et al. (2022)

In-context learning — Learning a pattern from the context, without changing a weight.

Loss on tokens later in a sequence is lower than loss on tokens earlier in it, because the model can use what it has already read. The induction-head paper argues that much of this is pattern completion by circuits like the one in the laboratory.

Olsson et al. (2022)

Name-mover head — The head that writes the answer name into the output.

In the IOI circuit, the name movers attend to the two names in the sentence and copy one of them to the final position. Which one they copy is decided upstream.

Wang et al. (2022)

S-inhibition head — The head that suppresses the wrong name.

It writes a signal that keeps the name movers from copying the subject, so the indirect object wins. It does not write the answer; it decides which of two candidates does.

Wang et al. (2022)

Completeness — How much of a behaviour the circuit reproduces.

Patch every node in the proposed circuit and measure how much of the behaviour comes back. A complete circuit accounts for the behaviour; an incomplete one leaves a residue it does not explain.

Wang et al. (2022)

Minimality — Whether every part of a circuit is needed.

Remove components one at a time and see whether the behaviour survives. A circuit can be complete and still contain components that are doing nothing for this behaviour.

Wang et al. (2022)

QK circuit — The product W_Qᵀ W_K, which decides which positions a head attends to.

One head reads the residual stream through two independent matrices, and this is the one that scores pairs of positions. It is the whole of the head’s where, and because it factorises out of the head it can be measured on its own — which is what makes a composed head’s influence patchable through its key input rather than through the head.

Elhage et al. (2021)

OV circuit — The product W_O W_V, which decides what a head writes for the positions it attends to.

Attention chooses the sources; W_O W_V chooses what is taken from each of them and written back into the stream. Because the head’s output is a sum over sources, its contribution to a logit splits into one term per position — the attention weight times the OV write projected on the readout — and that split is exact.

Elhage et al. (2021)

Path patching — Patching one head’s output into a single circuit input of another head.

Activation patching asks whether a component matters. Path patching asks which of its influences mattered: substitute the ablated head’s write into the query, key or value input of the later head, and the difference is that edge’s contribution. It is the tool that turns the framework’s paths into measurements.

Elhage et al. (2021)

Edge attribution — One edge’s marginal contribution to the graph that currently contains it.

Score an edge by what deleting it costs the graph, with all the other kept edges still in place. The score is a property of the edge and its neighbours, not of the edge alone: two edges that only work together each look essential while both are present. That is why a pruning search re-scores every remaining edge at every step.

Conmy et al. (2023)

ACDC — The search that deletes the least-scored component until the graph stops being faithful.

Given a metric and a behavioural gap: score every remaining node and edge by its marginal contribution, delete the smallest, repeat, and take as the answer the smallest graph that still cleared the threshold. Nothing is trained and no human chooses the components — which is why the method has to be graded on a model whose wiring is already known.

Conmy et al. (2023)

Appendix B — The laboratories

Every laboratory the course ships. Each one runs in the application and computes everything it shows in the browser; this appendix is the catalogue of what exists and what it is for.

A · Superposition

The interference, the threshold, and the trade-off curve between them.

Delivers:

  • Superposition in a tiny model
  • The price of a feature, computed exactly
  • The trade-off curve between interference and feature count

B · The sparse autoencoder

A dictionary, trained here — and what it does to a pair of overlapping features.

Delivers:

  • Training a sparse autoencoder on a tiny residual stream
  • L0 sparsity and reconstruction error
  • Feature splitting and absorption

C · Patching

From “responds to” to “does”.

Delivers:

  • Activation patching and the faithfulness score

D · One head, two circuits

The QK and OV circuits, and a head’s effect split exactly over its source positions.

Delivers:

  • Pathway decomposition of a single attention head

E · Composition and induction

Two heads, and the pattern one of them completes.

Delivers:

  • The two-head induction circuit, and the ablation of the previous-token head

F · Automated circuit discovery

Edge attribution scores, and ACDC pruning a graph down to the circuit.

Delivers:

  • Edge attribution scores

G · The four-step workflow

The paper’s procedure for finding a circuit, run on a model that can be checked.

Delivers:

  • The four-step workflow applied to the published IOI circuit

1. Judging with a Model

A strong model asked to pick the better of two answers

The central idea of model-based evaluation: instead of writing a reference answer, show a judge model two candidate answers and ask which is better. This module sets out the method, the measurement of how often it agrees with a human, and the consistency check that most people do not run.

Learning outcomes

  • State what an LLM-as-a-judge is asked to do, and what it is not asked to do
  • Measure agreement with a human and explain what the number means
  • Measure consistency under a permutation, and say why it is the harder test
  • Explain why the agreement number is a property of the question set as well as of the judge

Lesson 1. What a judge is asked to do

Two answers, one question, one preference

Estimated study time: 20 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the task the judge is given and the shape of its output
  • Explain why pairwise comparison is easier for a model than scoring
  • Say what the judge is not being asked to do

The ideas

  • The judge sees two answers to the same question and names the better one.
  • Pairwise comparison avoids writing a reference answer, which is where most benchmarks go wrong.
  • The judge is a model, so its preferences are the model’s preferences.

Practice

*Q. What is an LLM-as-a-judge asked to do? — multiple-choice (warmup)***

  • Score an answer against a reference answer
  • ✓ Choose between two candidate answers
  • Rewrite the answer to improve it
  • Check the answer against the ground truth

Correct.

Why: The judge sees a question and two answers and names the better one. The advantage over scoring against a reference is that no single phrasing has to be declared correct.

*Q. The judge’s preferences are the judge model’s preferences. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. A judge is a model, and whatever it has come to prefer — position, length, its own family’s style — comes through into every judgement it makes.

Go and do it

Measure how often a judge agrees with the human, and how often it agrees with itself. Open The judge against the human in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §2 MT-Bench and the judge · p. 4 — The judging prompt, the pairwise format, and the agreement measurement against human preference.
  • §1 Introduction · p. 1 — The claim that a strong model can substitute for human annotation, and the cost of that substitution.

The words this lesson uses

  • LLM-as-a-judge — Using a strong model to score or rank the outputs of other models.
  • Pairwise comparison — Choosing between two answers rather than scoring one.
  • Judge — The model that makes the comparison.
  • Agreement rate — How often the judge’s choice matches the human’s.

Lesson 2. Agreement and consistency

Two different numbers, and the second one is the harder test

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define agreement with a human and consistency under a permutation
  • Explain what a consistency failure tells you that a low agreement does not
  • Design the swap test

The ideas

  • Agreement is measured against a human; consistency is measured against the judge itself.
  • Swapping the two answers must not change the preference — and if it does, the judge is answering a different question.
  • A judge can be consistent and still be systematically wrong.

Practice

*Q. What does the position-swap test measure? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • How often the judge agrees with a human
  • ✓ How often the judge gives the same answer when the order is changed
  • How good the judge is at explaining itself
  • How expensive the judge is to run

Correct.

Why: Consistency is measured against the judge itself: the same pair, presented in both orders, should produce the same preference. A failure to do so means the judge answered a different question.

*Q. What does a consistency failure tell you that a low agreement with humans does not? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • That the judge is weak compared with humans
  • ✓ That the judge is not even a function of the answers — its verdict flips when the order is swapped
  • That the question set is too small
  • That humans disagree with each other

Correct — the swap test measures the judge against itself.

Why: Agreement is measured against a human; consistency is measured against the judge itself — the swap test reorders the two answers and asks again. A consistency failure means the verdicts are not a function of the answers alone, which no amount of agreement can repair.

Go and do it

Judge the same pair twice, with the positions swapped, and count the flips. Open The swap test in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §2 MT-Bench and the judge · p. 5 — The position-swap experiment and the consistency figures reported alongside the agreement rate.

The words this lesson uses

  • Consistency — How often the judge gives the same answer when the order is changed.
  • Position bias — A preference for the answer presented first.

Read first: What a judge is asked to do

2. The Biases of a Judge

Position, verbosity, and liking your own answers

A judge is a model, and models have preferences that have nothing to do with quality. This module takes the three biases the primary source measures, isolates each one, and measures it rather than describing it.

Learning outcomes

  • Define position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias
  • Design an experiment that isolates one bias
  • Read a consistency number and connect it to position bias
  • Say which of the three biases a pairwise protocol can fix for free

Lesson 3. Position bias

The answer in front of it

Estimated study time: 20 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define position bias and describe the swap test that detects it
  • Compute the rate at which a judge prefers the first position
  • Explain why a pairwise protocol can fix position bias for free

The ideas

  • A judge asked the same question twice, with the answers swapped, should answer differently.
  • A fair protocol presents each pair in both orders and takes the majority.
  • The cost is double the votes, which is why arenas that skip it look cheap.

Practice

*Q. How is position bias usually fixed? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ By presenting each pair in both orders and taking the majority
  • By making the judge stronger
  • By using a longer prompt
  • By scoring against a reference answer instead

Correct, at the cost of double the votes.

Why: Presenting both orders and taking the majority cancels a first-position preference exactly, because the bias then favours each answer equally often. It doubles the cost, which is why it is often skipped.

*Q. A judge prefers the first position in 62% of 1000 comparisons where the two answers are equally good. What is the excess preference, in percentage points? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 12 percentage points

Why: Exactly 12 percentage points above the 50% that a fair judge would show. That excess is the position bias, and it is what the swap test is for.

Go and do it

Count how often the judge prefers the answer in the first position. Open Measure the position preference in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §4 Limitations · p. 9 — The position bias measurement and the mitigation the paper proposes.

The words this lesson uses

  • Position bias — A preference for the answer presented first.
  • Consistency — How often the judge gives the same answer when the order is changed.

Read first: Agreement and consistency

Lesson 4. Verbosity and self-enhancement

Longer answers, and answers like mine

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias
  • Isolate each bias in an experiment
  • Say which of the two a protocol can fix and which it cannot

The ideas

  • A judge prefers the longer answer even when the shorter one is better.
  • A judge prefers answers from models similar to itself.
  • Neither bias is fixed by swapping positions; both have to be measured.

Practice

*Q. Which of these does the position-swap protocol NOT fix? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • Position bias
  • ✓ Verbosity bias
  • The order effect on the wording
  • A first-answer recency effect

Correct — swapping positions does nothing about a preference for length.

Why: The swap cancels anything that depends on position. A preference for longer answers does not depend on position, so it survives the swap intact and has to be measured separately.

*Q. Making the judge model stronger removes its verbosity bias. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: False

Why: No. The primary source reports that a stronger judge does not remove the bias. Scaling the judge does not scale away its preferences.

Go and do it

Hold the quality fixed, vary the length, and count the preference. Open Isolate the verbosity bias in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §4 Limitations · p. 9 — The verbosity bias and the self-enhancement bias, and the finding that a stronger judge does not remove them.

The words this lesson uses

  • Verbosity bias — A preference for the longer answer.
  • Self-enhancement bias — A preference for answers like the judge’s own.

Read first: Position bias

3. Human Agreement

What the agreement number actually tells you

An agreement rate of 80% sounds good and is often quoted without context. This module treats the number as what it is — a measurement with a denominator, a question set and a protocol — and asks what happens when the denominator changes.

Learning outcomes

  • Compute an agreement rate and identify its denominator
  • Explain why agreement and consistency are different numbers
  • Predict how a harder question set changes the agreement rate
  • Argue for reporting the judge against a human baseline rather than against 100%

Lesson 5. What an agreement rate means

The denominator is doing most of the work

Estimated study time: 20 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute an agreement rate and state its denominator
  • Explain why the same judge can score 65% or 85% on two question sets
  • Argue for a human baseline

The ideas

  • An agreement rate is a measurement with a denominator, and the denominator is a design decision.
  • On a question set where the answers are close, the judge will disagree with the human a lot — correctly.
  • The number to compare against is the agreement of two humans, not 100%.

Practice

*Q. Why does an agreement rate fall when the question set gets harder? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • The judge becomes less accurate
  • ✓ The answers get closer, so both the judge and the human are near a coin flip
  • Harder questions are longer, which activates the verbosity bias
  • Human annotators get tired

Correct.

Why: When the two answers are close in quality, the true preference is genuinely ambiguous, so a correct judge will often differ from a correct human. A low agreement on a hard set can mean the judge is right.

*Q. What is the right number to compare a judge’s agreement rate against? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • 100%
  • ✓ The agreement of two humans on the same question set
  • 50%
  • The judge’s score on a different benchmark

Correct.

Why: The inter-annotator agreement is the ceiling. A judge at 80% where humans agree with each other 85% is close to the best available measurement, not three-quarters of the way to perfect.

Go and do it

See how the agreement rate falls as the questions get harder. Open Agreement against difficulty in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §2 MT-Bench and the judge · p. 6 — The agreement rate of 80.9% against human preference, and the comparison with the inter-annotator agreement.
  • §1 Introduction · p. 2 — The claim that a judge can reach agreement with experts, and the conditions under which it holds.

The words this lesson uses

  • Agreement rate — How often the judge’s choice matches the human’s.
  • Human baseline — How often two humans agree with each other.

Read first: What a judge is asked to do

4. Arena Rankings

Turning pairwise votes into a leaderboard

An arena collects votes and produces a ranking. This module covers the Bradley–Terry model that Chatbot Arena uses, the confidence interval that should accompany it, and the cost of a vote — which is what limits how precise a leaderboard can be.

Learning outcomes

  • Fit a Bradley–Terry model to pairwise votes and read the strengths
  • Compute a bootstrap confidence interval on a ranking
  • Explain why an Elo rating is not a confidence interval
  • Estimate how many votes it takes to separate two models

Lesson 6. From votes to a ranking

The Bradley–Terry model

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the Bradley–Terry model and its likelihood
  • Explain why the strengths are only identified up to a constant
  • Read a fitted ranking and say what the strengths mean

The ideas

  • Pr(i beats j) = σ(θ_i − θ_j): one number per model, one difference per comparison.
  • The likelihood is a sum of logarithms, and it can be maximised directly.
  • The model is fitted by maximum likelihood, not by an update rule.

Practice

*Q. In the Bradley–Terry model, what does the strength θ_i represent? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • The number of votes model i received
  • ✓ A number such that the chance of i beating j depends on θ_i − θ_j
  • The accuracy of model i on the benchmark
  • The cost of one vote for model i

Correct.

Why: Pr(i beats j) = σ(θ_i − θ_j). The strength is not a count of votes; it is the parameter of the difference, and the model says a pair of votes for i and one for j is worth more than a tie.

*Q. In a Bradley–Terry model with strengths θ_A = 1 and θ_B = 0, what is the probability that A beats B? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 0.7310586 ± 0.0001

Why: σ(1 − 0) = 1/(1 + e⁻¹) ≈ 0.731. Note that it is not 0.5: a strength difference of one already gives a clear favourite.

Go and do it

Collect the votes and fit a Bradley–Terry model to them. Open Fit a ranking to the votes in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §3 Chatbot Arena · p. 7 — The Bradley–Terry model behind the arena ranking, and the bootstrap confidence intervals reported with it.
  • §3 Chatbot Arena · p. 8 — The cost of the votes, and the observation that the number of votes per model varies widely.

The words this lesson uses

  • Bradley–Terry model — A model in which each item has a strength, and the chance of i beating j is a function of the difference.
  • Elo — An online rating update for pairwise comparisons.
  • Arena — A platform where users compare two models and vote.

Read first: What a judge is asked to do

Lesson 7. The interval and the cost

How precise is a leaderboard, and what does precision cost?

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute a bootstrap interval on a fitted ranking
  • Explain why an Elo rating is not an interval
  • Estimate the number of votes needed to separate two models

The ideas

  • Resampling the votes and refitting gives an interval on the ranking.
  • Elo is an online update rule, so its result depends on the order the votes arrived in.
  • Votes are not free, and the price of precision is the thing that limits a leaderboard.

Practice

*Q. Why is an Elo rating not a confidence interval? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • Elo ratings are not computed from votes
  • ✓ Elo is an online update, so its result depends on the order the votes arrived in
  • Elo assumes the models are equally good to start
  • Elo cannot handle draws

Correct.

Why: A bootstrap interval resamples the votes and refits, and it means the same thing whatever order they arrived in. An online rating carries the path with it.

*Q. Why is an Elo rating alone not an interval? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • Because Elo is only defined for chess
  • ✓ Because the rating is a point estimate from one fit — resampling the votes and refitting is what produces the interval
  • Because Elo cannot be computed from pairwise votes
  • Because the interval would be too wide to publish

Correct — the bootstrap is what turns the ranking into a measurement with width.

Why: Resampling the votes and refitting gives an interval on the ranking — which is what separates two models whose ratings differ. And the number of votes needed to separate them grows with how close they are, which is the cost half of the lesson.

Go and do it

Watch the confidence interval on the top two models shrink as the votes accumulate. Open How many votes to tell them apart in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §3 Chatbot Arena · p. 8 — The bootstrap procedure and the reported intervals on the arena ranking.
  • §3 Chatbot Arena · p. 8 — The cost of the votes: how many are needed before the ranking stabilises.

The words this lesson uses

  • Bootstrap — Resampling the data with replacement, many times, to get an interval.
  • Confidence interval — A range that a measurement plausibly lies in.
  • Elo — An online rating update for pairwise comparisons.

Read first: From votes to a ranking

5. Benchmark Design

What you put in the question set decides what comes out

A benchmark is a measurement instrument, and instruments have design decisions. This module covers contamination — what happens when the test set is in the training set — and the way contamination moves a ranking more than it moves a score.

Learning outcomes

  • Compute the score inflation a contamination fraction produces
  • Explain why differential contamination moves rankings more than scores
  • Say what a benchmark author should do about it
  • Distinguish contamination from saturation and from overfitting

Lesson 8. Contamination

When the test set is in the training set

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute the score inflation a contamination fraction produces
  • Explain why differential contamination moves rankings more than scores
  • Distinguish contamination from saturation and from overfitting

The ideas

  • A contaminated question is answered from memory rather than from capability.
  • The score inflation is proportional to the contaminated fraction.
  • When only some models are contaminated, the ranking moves more than any single score.

Practice

*Q. A benchmark has 200 questions and a model scores 60% on them. 10% of the questions are contaminated and on those the model scores 90% instead of 60%. What is the reported score? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 63 percent

Why: Exactly 63%. Twenty contaminated questions at 90% contribute 18 successes where 12 were expected, and 180 clean ones at 60% contribute 108: (18 + 108) / 200 = 0.63. The inflation is 3 percentage points.

*Q. Why can contamination move a ranking more than it moves any single score? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • Because contamination inflates every model equally
  • ✓ Because contamination is usually differential: one model has seen the benchmark and the others have not
  • Because the error bars shrink under contamination
  • Because rankings are computed from fewer votes

Correct.

Why: A common shift changes every model’s score by the same amount and leaves the order alone. A differential shift — one model contaminated, the others not — is precisely a change in the order.

Go and do it

Sweep the contaminated fraction and watch the reported score drift. Open What contamination does to a score in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §6 Conclusion · p. 12 — The paper’s statement of what the method does not address, including the contamination question.

Further reading

  • The Leaderboard Illusion, arXiv:2504.20879 — The newest and sharpest criticism of the evaluation ecosystem.

The words this lesson uses

  • Contamination — Test questions that appear in the training data.
  • Benchmark — A fixed question set with a scoring procedure.
  • Saturation — A benchmark every strong model solves.

Lesson 9. What a benchmark is for

Two things it has to do at once

Estimated study time: 20 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the two things a benchmark has to do at once
  • Explain the tension between breadth and depth in a question set
  • Say what the holistic framing adds to a single score

The ideas

  • A benchmark has to be hard enough to separate models and easy enough to run.
  • A single number hides the trade-offs; a set of numbers shows them.
  • The question set is a claim about what matters, and it should be argued for.

Practice

*Q. Which of these are design decisions a benchmark author makes? — multi-select (core)***

  • ✓ Which questions to ask
  • ✓ How the answers are scored
  • What the score is called
  • ✓ Which models are evaluated

Why: The question set, the scoring procedure and the set of models under test are all choices. Each one is a claim about what matters, and each one can be argued for.

*Q. What two things does a benchmark have to do at once? — multiple-choice (warmup)***

  • Be cheap to run and easy to cite
  • ✓ Be hard enough to separate models and easy enough to run
  • Be fully automatic and fully adversarial
  • Cover every capability and reject every bad model

Correct — the tension between breadth and depth lives between them.

Why: A benchmark has to be hard enough to separate models and easy enough to run. The question set lives in that tension: breadth buys coverage, depth buys discrimination, and the holistic framing is what a single score adds to the pair.

Go and do it

See how the difficulty mix of a question set changes what the score measures. Open Build a question set in the evaluation-lab application.

Further reading

  • HELM, arXiv:2211.09110 — The multi-metric, multi-scenario alternative to a single score.

The words this lesson uses

  • Benchmark — A fixed question set with a scoring procedure.
  • Holistic evaluation — Measuring many scenarios on many metrics instead of one number.

Read first: Contamination

6. Measurement

The number on the leaderboard has an error bar

A score from N questions is a proportion, and a proportion has a standard error. This module computes it, shows how the interval narrows, and asks how many questions you need to tell two models apart — a question that is usually not asked.

Learning outcomes

  • Compute the standard error of a benchmark score
  • Explain why the interval narrows as one over the square root of N
  • Compute the number of questions needed to detect a given difference
  • Argue for publishing an interval next to every score

Lesson 10. The standard error

The number that should be next to the score

Estimated study time: 20 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute the standard error of a benchmark score
  • Explain the one-over-the-square-root-of-N rule
  • Argue for publishing the interval with the score

The ideas

  • A score from N binary outcomes is a proportion, with variance p(1−p)/N.
  • To halve the interval you need four times as many questions.
  • A difference smaller than the interval is not a difference.

Practice

*Q. A model scores 50% on a benchmark of 400 questions. What is the standard error of that score? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 0.0125 ± 0.0001

Why: √(0.5 × 0.5 / 400) = √(0.000625) = 0.0125. The 95% interval is therefore roughly 50% ± 2.5 percentage points.

*Q. To halve the width of a confidence interval, how many times more questions are needed? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • Twice as many
  • ✓ Four times as many
  • Ten times as many
  • Half as many

Correct.

Why: The width goes as 1/√N, so halving it needs N to grow by a factor of four. This is the arithmetic behind why large benchmarks are expensive.

Go and do it

Plot the width of the confidence interval against the number of questions. Open How the interval narrows in the evaluation-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §5 Related work · p. 11 — Where the paper situates itself among the measurement-based approaches to evaluation.

Further reading

  • Lessons from the Trenches, arXiv:2405.14782 — The practical failure modes: seeds, decoders, chat templates, and how much each one moves a score.

The words this lesson uses

  • Standard error — How much a measurement of this kind wobbles around its true value.
  • Confidence interval — A range that a measurement plausibly lies in.

Lesson 11. How many questions

The question nobody asks before the benchmark is released

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute the number of questions needed to detect a given difference
  • Explain the power of a comparison
  • Say what happens when the difference you care about is smaller than the noise

The ideas

  • The number of questions needed grows as the square of the inverse of the difference.
  • A benchmark that cannot detect the difference you care about is not measuring it.
  • Halving the effect size quadruples the cost.

Practice

*Q. A benchmark with very low power will report real differences as ties. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. If the test cannot detect the difference, the difference does not appear — and a leaderboard that reports a tie there is reporting an artefact of the question count.

*Q. The number of questions needed grows as the square of the inverse of the difference. If the difference you care about doubles, by what factor does the required question count fall? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 0.25 ± 0.001

Why: The count scales as 1/difference², so doubling the difference divides the required count by four. And when the difference you care about is smaller than the noise, no affordable question count answers it — which is the finding, not a failure to produce one.

Go and do it

Compute how many questions a given difference needs, and watch the curve. Open The cost of detecting a small difference in the evaluation-lab application.

The words this lesson uses

  • Power — The probability of detecting a real difference if there is one.
  • Standard error — How much a measurement of this kind wobbles around its true value.

Read first: The standard error

Lesson 12. What to publish

The minimum a leaderboard should print

Estimated study time: 18 minutes

What you will learn

  • List what a leaderboard should print next to every score
  • Explain why the question count belongs there
  • Argue for reporting the judge against a human baseline

The ideas

  • A score without an interval is a claim, not a measurement.
  • A score without a question count cannot be compared with anything.
  • A score without the protocol cannot be reproduced.

Practice

*Q. What should a leaderboard print next to every score? — multi-select (hard)***

  • ✓ A confidence interval
  • ✓ The number of questions used
  • ✓ The provider of the model
  • The logo of the organisation that ran it

Why: An interval, the question count, and enough about the protocol to reproduce it. The newest criticism of the field is that the last of these is often missing, and that the leaderboard has become the thing being optimised.

*Q. Which of these should a leaderboard print next to every score? — multi-select (core)***

  • ✓ The interval on the score
  • ✓ The number of questions the score was computed on
  • ✓ The judge’s agreement with a human baseline
  • The judge’s own self-evaluation score

Why: A score without an interval is a claim, not a measurement; the question count is where the width comes from; and the judge’s agreement with a human baseline is the number that says what the whole instrument is worth.

Go and do it

The same score, with and without its interval, and what a reader can conclude from each. Open What the interval looks like in the evaluation-lab application.

The words this lesson uses

  • Confidence interval — A range that a measurement plausibly lies in.
  • Human baseline — How often two humans agree with each other.

Read first: How many questions

Appendix A — Glossary

LLM-as-a-judge — Using a strong model to score or rank the outputs of other models.

The method: give a strong model the question and one or more candidate answers, and ask it which is better. It replaces most of the human annotation a benchmark would otherwise need, and it inherits the judge’s own preferences along with its judgement.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Judge — The model that makes the comparison.

In this course the judge is a synthetic model with known, injected biases, because that is how a bias can be measured rather than merely suspected. The protocol is identical to the one used with a real judge.

Course term

Pairwise comparison — Choosing between two answers rather than scoring one.

The pairwise protocol is much easier for a model than open-ended scoring, because there is no scale to calibrate: the judge only has to express a preference between two things it can read side by side.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Agreement rate — How often the judge’s choice matches the human’s.

A proportion, and like every proportion it has a denominator that is a design decision. The same judge on the same answers can score 65% or 85% depending on how close the answers were.

Example: What does an 80% agreement rate mean? → That on the questions used, the judge and the human picked the same answer four times out of five — and it says nothing about the other fifteen percent, or about any other question set.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Consistency — How often the judge gives the same answer when the order is changed.

Consistency is measured by judging the same pair twice with the positions swapped and checking whether the same answer was preferred. A judge can be perfectly consistent and still systematically prefer the longer answer.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Position bias — A preference for the answer presented first.

The most cited of the judge’s biases. It is detected by the swap test, and it is fixed for free by presenting every pair in both orders and taking the majority — which doubles the cost of the evaluation.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Verbosity bias — A preference for the longer answer.

A judge that prefers length will prefer whichever model writes more, whatever the quality. It is not fixed by swapping positions, and it does not go away when the judge is made stronger.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Self-enhancement bias — A preference for answers like the judge’s own.

A judge tends to prefer the outputs of models in its own family. The effect is asymmetric: an own-family answer gets the benefit of the doubt and the other one does not.

Zheng et al. (2023)

Human baseline — How often two humans agree with each other.

The number a judge’s agreement rate should be compared against. Human annotators disagree with each other too, so 100% is the wrong target and a judge at 80% may be close to the ceiling.

Course term

Arena — A platform where users compare two models and vote.

An arena produces pairwise votes at scale, from real users, on prompts nobody wrote. The votes are then turned into a ranking. What the arena measures is what people prefer, which is not the same as what is correct.

Chiang et al. (2024)

Bradley–Terry model — A model in which each item has a strength, and the chance of i beating j is a function of the difference.

Pr(i beats j) = σ(θ_i − θ_j). One number per model, one difference per comparison. It is fitted by maximum likelihood, and its strengths are only identified up to an additive constant.

Example: Why must the strengths sum to zero? → Because adding a constant to every strength leaves every difference — and therefore every probability — unchanged. The offset is arbitrary.

Chiang et al. (2024)

Elo — An online rating update for pairwise comparisons.

Each comparison updates two ratings by an amount proportional to how far the result was from what the ratings predicted. Because it is an online rule, the final ratings depend on the order the votes arrived in, and Elo ratings are not confidence intervals.

Chiang et al. (2024)

Bootstrap — Resampling the data with replacement, many times, to get an interval.

Resample the votes, refit the model, and look at the spread of the answers. It makes no assumption about the distribution of the estimates, which is why it is the method the arena uses.

Chiang et al. (2024)

Confidence interval — A range that a measurement plausibly lies in.

For a benchmark score it is the score plus and minus about 1.96 standard errors. A leaderboard that prints a score without an interval is printing a point estimate as if it were a fact.

Course term

Standard error — How much a measurement of this kind wobbles around its true value.

A score from N binary outcomes with a true pass rate p has standard error √(p(1−p)/N). It falls as one over the square root of N, which is the single most useful fact about benchmark design.

Example: A score of 70% on 100 questions: what is the standard error? → √(0.7 × 0.3 / 100) ≈ 0.046, so roughly ±9% at 95%.

Course term

Power — The probability of detecting a real difference if there is one.

A benchmark with low power will miss real differences, and will report them as ties. Power rises with the number of questions and falls with the square of the effect size.

Course term

Benchmark — A fixed question set with a scoring procedure.

Two design decisions in one artefact: what to ask, and how to score the answer. Both are claims about what matters, and a benchmark that does not argue for them is not a measurement so much as a preference.

Liang et al. (2023)

Contamination — Test questions that appear in the training data.

A contaminated question is answered from memory rather than from capability. The score inflation is proportional to the contaminated fraction, and it is invisible unless you know that fraction.

Course term

Saturation — A benchmark every strong model solves.

Once the scores cluster at the ceiling, the benchmark stops separating models and the remaining differences become noise. Saturation is a design failure, not a success.

Course term

Holistic evaluation — Measuring many scenarios on many metrics instead of one number.

The alternative to a single leaderboard score. It is more informative and much more work, and the argument it makes is that the trade-offs between scenarios are the interesting part.

Liang et al. (2023)

Leaderboard — A published table of models and their scores.

A leaderboard is a measurement instrument that publishes its readings without its error bars. The newest criticism of the field is that the leaderboards themselves have become the thing being optimised.

Singh et al. (2025)

Reference answer — The gold standard an answer is scored against.

A benchmark that scores against a reference answer is measuring similarity to one particular phrasing. Pairwise comparison avoids that, at the cost of needing something to compare against.

Course term

Reproducibility — Whether the same code, seed and prompt give the same score.

A benchmark whose score moves when the decoding seed changes, or when the chat template changes, is not measuring the model. The trench-level detail is unglamorous and it is most of the problem.

Reuel et al. (2024)

Difficulty — How hard a question is, and therefore how close the answers are.

The single best predictor of a judge’s agreement rate. When the answers are close, the human and the judge are both near a coin flip, and the agreement rate falls.

Course term

Question set — The prompts a benchmark asks.

Its composition — how many are easy, how many are hard, which domains they cover — determines what the score means. A score is a statement about the question set at least as much as about the model.

Course term

Model family — A group of models trained in the same way, which look alike.

Judges are biased towards their own family, so a leaderboard that mixes families and a judge that only knows one of them will produce a ranking that reflects the judge’s taste.

Course term

Inter-annotator agreement — How much two people agree.

The ceiling for any automated evaluation of the same data. It is the honest target for a judge, and it is usually well below 100%, because the task is genuinely ambiguous.

Course term

Permutation — A reordering of the two answers in a pairwise comparison.

Presenting the same pair in both orders and checking whether the judge’s choice follows the answer or the position is the standard test for position bias, and the standard mitigation.

Course term

Vote — One pairwise comparison, cast by one voter.

The unit of an arena. Votes are not free — they cost the platform money per model queried — and that cost is what bounds how precise a leaderboard can be.

Chiang et al. (2024)

Contamination fraction — The proportion of a benchmark that appears in the training data.

The score inflation it produces is the fraction times the per-question inflation. Nobody knows this number, which is exactly why a contaminated score cannot be trusted.

Course term

1. Policy Gradients

Optimising a distribution by moving its log-probabilities

RLHF optimises a policy, not a function. This module introduces the objective — the expected reward of the policy — and the estimator that makes it tractable: the score-function trick, which replaces a derivative through the model with a weighted log-probability.

Learning outcomes

  • State the objective RLHF maximises and why it is an expectation over a distribution
  • Write the score-function estimator and explain what replaced the derivative
  • Verify a policy gradient against a finite difference on a problem where the answer is known

Lesson 1. The objective

Maximising an expectation over a distribution you are also changing

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the objective an RLHF pipeline maximises
  • Explain why the gradient of an expectation is not the expectation of the gradient
  • Compute the expected reward of a policy on a finite problem exactly

The ideas

  • The objective is E_{a~π}[r(a)] — a number that depends on the whole distribution.
  • Moving the policy changes which actions are sampled, so the derivative has to account for that.
  • On a finite problem the expectation is a finite sum, and its gradient is available exactly.

Practice

*Q. What does an RLHF policy stage maximise? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The expected reward under the policy, minus a KL penalty
  • The reward of the single best response
  • The likelihood of the reference responses
  • The log-probability of the policy’s samples

Correct.

Why: The objective is an expectation over the actions the policy samples, minus a penalty for moving away from the reference. The penalty is part of the objective, not a regulariser bolted on afterwards.

*Q. The gradient of an expectation is the expectation of the gradient. — boolean (core)***

Answer: False

Why: No — and this is the whole reason the score-function estimator exists. The distribution is being moved, so the derivative has to account for that. The score-function estimator is the identity that makes it possible without differentiating through the model.

Go and do it

Compute the expected reward of a policy and check its gradient against a finite difference. Open The expected reward and its gradient in the rlhf-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §2 Background: PPO and the RLHF pipeline · p. 3 — The three stages of the pipeline and the objective the policy stage optimises.

The words this lesson uses

  • Policy — A distribution over actions, given a state.
  • Policy gradient — The gradient of the expected reward with respect to the policy’s parameters.
  • Objective — The quantity the training maximises.
  • Expectation — The average of a random variable over its distribution.

Lesson 2. The estimator

The derivative you do not have to take

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the score-function estimator
  • Explain what it costs to be unbiased instead of low-variance
  • State the conditions the estimator needs

The ideas

  • ∇E_π[r] = E_π[r · ∇log π] — the model’s own log-probability replaces its derivative.
  • The trick needs the support of π to be unchanged as the parameters move.
  • The estimator is unbiased but high-variance, which is what the value function is for.

Practice

*Q. What does the score-function estimator replace? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The derivative of the model, with its own log-probability
  • The reward, with the value function
  • The expectation, with a sample
  • The KL penalty, with a constraint

Correct.

Why: ∇E_π[r] = E_π[r · ∇log π]. The model’s own log-probability stands in for the model’s derivative, which is what makes the estimator possible for a language model whose output layer is enormous.

*Q. The score-function estimator needs the support of the policy to stay unchanged. What goes wrong for an action the policy would never sample? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Its log-probability is undefined, so the action can never be sampled and never be credited
  • The reward becomes negative
  • The variance doubles
  • The KL penalty stops applying

Correct — the estimator reweights what was actually drawn; an unsampled action contributes nothing, however good it is.

Why: The gradient identity ∇E_π[r] = E_π[r · ∇log π] reweights the actions the policy actually drew. Where π(a) = 0, ∇log π(a) does not exist, and no amount of training can move probability onto an action the estimator has never seen — which is why exploration has to come from somewhere else.

Go and do it

Compare the score-function estimator with the exact gradient of a finite problem. Open The estimator against the exact gradient in the rlhf-lab application.

Further reading

  • Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction — The policy gradient theorem, from first principles.

The words this lesson uses

  • Score-function estimator — ∇E_π[r] = E_π[r · ∇log π] — the derivative without the derivative.
  • Baseline — A constant subtracted from the reward without changing the gradient.
  • Variance — How much an estimator’s answer moves between runs.

Read first: The objective

2. Trust Regions

Bounding how far one update may move the policy

Taking a large step in the space of policies destroys the policy: the samples that justified the old estimate no longer represent the new one. This module covers the constraint that prevents it, and the algorithm that made it practical.

Learning outcomes

  • Write the trust-region constraint and say what it is for
  • Explain why a KL penalty and a KL constraint are not the same thing
  • Describe the natural gradient and the conjugate-gradient step that replaces it

Lesson 3. The trust region

Bounding the step, not the reward

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the trust-region constraint
  • Explain what a large step does to the samples that justified the old estimate
  • Distinguish a KL penalty from a KL constraint

The ideas

  • The constraint is on the KL between the old and new policies, not on the objective.
  • A KL penalty is a soft nudge; a KL constraint is a hard boundary that the optimiser respects.
  • The bound is what makes the importance ratio a usable estimate of the new policy.

Practice

*Q. What is the purpose of the trust-region constraint? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ To keep the samples that justified the old estimate valid
  • To stop the policy from producing low-probability text
  • To make the reward model more accurate
  • To keep the loss from diverging

Correct.

Why: The importance ratio is only a usable correction while the two policies are close. A large step makes the collected samples a poor description of the new policy, and the estimate silently becomes wrong.

*Q. How is a KL penalty different from a KL constraint? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ A penalty is a soft term in the objective; a constraint is a boundary the optimiser respects
  • They are the same thing with different names
  • A penalty is computed exactly and a constraint is estimated
  • A constraint is a regulariser and a penalty is a hyperparameter

Correct.

Why: A penalty trades reward against distance at whatever ratio the coefficient sets. A constraint says the distance may not exceed δ, and the optimiser adjusts the step to respect it.

Go and do it

Watch the KL between the old and new policies as the step size grows. Open How far a step moves the policy in the rlhf-lab application.

Further reading

  • Schulman et al., arXiv:1502.05477 — TRPO: the constraint, the natural gradient, and the conjugate-gradient step.

The words this lesson uses

  • Trust region — A constraint on how far the new policy may be from the old one.
  • Importance ratio — The ratio of the new policy’s probability to the old one’s.
  • Natural gradient — The gradient measured in the geometry of the distribution.

Read first: The estimator

3. Proximal Policy Optimization

The clipped surrogate, and what the clip actually does

PPO replaces the hard constraint with a clip: once the importance ratio passes a bound, the objective stops rewarding movement in that direction. This module derives the objective, shows exactly when the clip bites, and covers the advantage estimate that goes with it.

Learning outcomes

  • Write the clipped surrogate and identify the region where the gradient vanishes
  • Compute the clip fraction and say what it measures
  • Explain why a step that is clipped has zero gradient rather than a smaller one
  • Derive generalised advantage estimation from the one-step residual

Lesson 5. The clipped objective

Where the gradient goes to zero

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the clipped surrogate and find the region where the clip is active
  • Explain why a clipped step has zero gradient rather than a smaller one
  • Compute the clip fraction and say what it is for

The ideas

  • The objective takes the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms.
  • When the clip is active the objective is flat, so its gradient is exactly zero.
  • The clip fraction is the diagnostic: it should fall as training goes well.

Practice

*Q. What happens to the gradient of the clipped objective when the clip is active? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It becomes exactly zero
  • It becomes smaller but stays non-zero
  • It is clipped to a small value
  • It is rescaled by the clip factor

Correct.

Why: Where the clip is active the objective is min(clipped, unclipped) and the clipped branch is the smaller one — and it is a constant. The gradient is therefore exactly zero, not merely small. That is the mechanism: the step is discarded, not shrunk.

*Q. With ε = 0.2, what is the clipped objective when the importance ratio is 2.0 and the advantage is 1? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 1.2

Why: Exactly 1.2. The ratio is clipped to 1 + ε = 1.2, and the minimum of the two branches is the clipped one, because the advantage is positive.

*Q. When the PPO clip is active, the gradient of the objective with respect to the policy is exactly zero. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: The objective takes the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms. On the segment where the clip is doing the work, the objective is locally constant, so its gradient vanishes — the policy is simply not pushed further in that direction, which is how the clip acts as a trust region.

Go and do it

Sweep the importance ratio and watch the objective and its gradient change. Open Where the clip bites in the rlhf-lab application.

The words this lesson uses

  • Clipped surrogate objective — The PPO objective: the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms.
  • Clip fraction — The fraction of steps where the clip was active.
  • Importance ratio — The ratio of the new policy’s probability to the old one’s.

Lesson 6. Advantages and GAE

The credit assignment, and its one hyperparameter

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the one-step temporal-difference residual
  • Derive generalised advantage estimation from it
  • Explain the bias–variance trade-off that λ controls

The ideas

  • δ_t = r_t + γV(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t) is the one-step surprise.
  • GAE sums the residuals with a geometric discount, and λ sets how far it looks.
  • λ = 0 is the one-step estimate; λ = 1 is the Monte Carlo return.

Practice

*Q. What does λ = 1 in generalised advantage estimation give? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The Monte Carlo return, minus the baseline
  • The one-step temporal-difference residual
  • The importance ratio
  • Zero

Correct: unbiased, high variance.

Why: λ = 1 makes the geometric sum telescope into the discounted return. It is unbiased and noisy; λ = 0 is the one-step residual, which is tight and biased.

*Q. In GAE, what does the estimator at λ = 1 recover? — multiple-choice (warmup)***

  • The one-step TD error
  • ✓ The Monte Carlo return
  • The reward model’s raw score
  • Zero, whatever the data says

Correct — full lookahead, high variance, no bias from the value function.

Why: GAE sums the one-step residuals with a geometric discount. λ = 0 trusts the value function alone; λ = 1 trusts the sampled returns alone — the Monte Carlo estimate, with its variance.

Go and do it

Move λ and watch the advantage estimate move from the one-step residual to the Monte Carlo return. Open The bias–variance trade-off in λ in the rlhf-lab application.

  • §4 Implementation details · p. 8 — The advantage estimator and the discount among the enumerated details.

The words this lesson uses

  • Advantage — How much better an action was than the average action in that state.
  • Generalised advantage estimation — A geometric sum of the one-step residuals, with λ setting how far it looks.
  • Value function — The expected return from a state, under the current policy.

4. The KL Penalty

What keeps the aligned model recognisably itself

The penalty term is the KL divergence from the supervised reference policy, and it has to be estimated from samples. This module compares the three estimators in common use, shows which of them is unbiased for what, and explains why the right choice depends on whether the KL is a penalty or a report.

Learning outcomes

  • State why the penalty is measured from the reference policy
  • Compare the three KL estimators and say what each is unbiased for
  • Explain why a penalty has to be non-negative and a reported number does not

Lesson 4. The KL penalty

A number that has to be estimated from samples

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • State what the penalty measures and against what
  • Write the three estimators and say what each is unbiased for
  • Explain why a penalty must be non-negative

The ideas

  • The penalty is the KL from the reference policy, and it is a sample estimate.
  • The naive estimator is unbiased but can be negative; the squared one is positive but biased.
  • The third estimator is positive, and its expectation is the chi-square divergence minus the KL — a detail most write-ups leave out.

Practice

*Q. Which of the three KL estimators is unbiased for the KL divergence? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ The log-ratio, k1
  • The squared log-ratio, k2
  • r − 1 − log r, k3
  • None of them

Correct — but it can be negative, which is why it is not used as a penalty.

Why: E_π[log(π/π_ref)] is exactly the KL. The other two are used for different reasons: k2 because it is positive, k3 because it is positive and has lower variance — not because it is unbiased for the KL.

*Q. A policy puts probability 0.5 on an action and the reference puts 0.25 on it. What is the log-ratio, in nats? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 0.6931472 ± 0.0001

Why: log(0.5/0.25) = log 2 ≈ 0.693 nats. The k3 estimator on the same sample would be 2 − 1 − log 2 ≈ 0.307.

*Q. The sample estimator of the KL that practitioners actually record is the third one. What is true of it? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • It is negative at almost every sample
  • ✓ It is pointwise positive, and its expectation is the chi-square divergence minus the KL
  • It equals the KL exactly, sample by sample
  • It needs the reward model to evaluate

Correct — a detail most write-ups leave out.

Why: The naive estimator can be negative sample by sample, and the squared replacement is positive but biased. The third estimator is pointwise positive, and its expectation is the chi-square divergence minus the KL — which is why curves drawn with it need that caveat read before them.

Go and do it

Estimate the KL three ways and compare each against the quantity it is actually unbiased for. Open The three estimators, measured in the rlhf-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §4 Implementation details · p. 8 — The KL estimator and the coefficient, among the enumerated details that decide whether training works.

The words this lesson uses

  • KL penalty — A term subtracted from the reward to keep the policy near the reference.
  • Reference policy — The policy the KL is measured against — normally the supervised model.
  • The k3 estimator — r − 1 − log r, which is always non-negative.

5. The N+ Details

What had to be true for the pipeline to train at all

The primary source’s contribution is an enumeration: twenty implementation details, each of which was found to matter, and a reproduction that only worked with most of them in place. This module treats that list as a checklist of the failure modes of RLHF training.

Learning outcomes

  • Name the stages of an RLHF pipeline and the failure mode of each
  • Explain why the scale of the reward model’s error decides how far the policy can be pushed
  • Argue for the checklist as a way of reporting a training result

Lesson 7. The three stages

Supervised, then ranked, then optimised

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Name the three stages of an RLHF pipeline and what each produces
  • Say what each stage can fail at
  • Explain why the reference policy comes from the first stage

The ideas

  • The supervised stage produces the reference policy that the penalty is measured against.
  • The reward stage produces a ranking of responses, which is what the third stage consumes.
  • The third stage optimises a policy against a proxy, and that is where the danger is.

Practice

*Q. Which stage of the RLHF pipeline produces the reference policy? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Supervised fine-tuning
  • Reward modelling
  • Policy optimisation
  • Evaluation

Correct.

Why: The reference policy is the supervised model. The KL penalty is measured against it, so the reference decides both the direction and the size of the movement the third stage is allowed.

*Q. What does the reward model produce? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ A scalar score for a response
  • A new policy
  • A preference between two responses
  • A dataset

Correct, and the score is wrong in a way that matters.

Why: A scalar per response, trained from pairwise preferences. The third stage then maximises the expected score — and the error in that score is what makes overoptimisation possible.

Twenty details, and the argument for listing them

Answer: False

*Q. Which of these does the primary source’s enumeration treat as implementation details that a reproducible result must state? — multi-select (core)***

  • ✓ The number of PPO epochs run per batch
  • ✓ How the KL penalty is managed while training proceeds
  • Whether RLHF is the right paradigm at all

Why: The paper’s contribution is an enumeration, and most of it is about scale: the reward model’s noise, the learning rates, the epochs, the KL management. Whether the paradigm is right is not a detail of the pipeline — it is a different paper.

6. Reward Overoptimisation

The point where optimising harder makes things worse

A reward model is a proxy, and a proxy that is optimised past its accuracy stops being informative. This module builds the phenomenon exactly rather than describing it, and fits the two functional forms the overoptimisation paper reports.

Learning outcomes

  • State the overoptimisation result and why a fixed-size proxy error is enough to cause it
  • Compare reinforcement learning and best-of-n against the same proxy
  • Fit and read the two functional forms the paper reports
  • Explain what the turning point of the curve means operationally

Lesson 9. The overoptimisation result

Goodhart, with a curve

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the result: optimising a proxy harder eventually makes the true reward worse
  • Explain why a fixed-size proxy error is enough to cause it
  • Read the turning point of the curve operationally

The ideas

  • The proxy error does not grow as you push harder, so the gap between the proxy and the truth opens up.
  • The true reward is maximised at a finite distance from the reference, not at infinity.
  • Past that point, every unit of proxy reward costs more true reward than it gains.

Practice

*Q. What is the overoptimisation result? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Optimising a proxy reward harder eventually makes the true reward worse
  • A bigger reward model always gives a better policy
  • Reward models cannot be trained at all
  • The KL penalty should be removed

Correct.

Why: The true reward is maximised at a finite distance from the reference. Past that point every unit of proxy reward costs more true reward than it gains — which is Goodhart’s law with a curve attached.

*Q. Why is a fixed-size reward-model error enough to cause overoptimisation? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ Because the error does not grow as the policy is pushed, so the gap between proxy and truth opens up
  • Because the error is random and noise is always harmful
  • Because a fixed error makes the reward model worse over time
  • Because the KL penalty grows with the error

Correct.

Why: The proxy’s error is a fixed landscape. Pushing the policy further finds the high spots in that landscape, and the further you go the more the proxy is rewarding its own noise rather than the truth.

Go and do it

Push the policy further and watch the proxy rise while the true reward turns over. Open The curve in the rlhf-lab application.

The words this lesson uses

  • Overoptimisation — The point past which optimising a proxy makes the true objective worse.
  • Goodhart’s law — When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
  • Proxy reward — The reward model’s score, standing in for the thing you actually care about.

Lesson 10. The functional forms

Two curves, fitted to a curve

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Write the two functional forms the overoptimisation paper reports
  • Fit them to a controlled setting and read the fit
  • Compare reinforcement learning against best-of-n on the same proxy

The ideas

  • For best-of-n: R(d) = d(α − β d), a downward parabola through the origin.
  • For reinforcement learning: R(d) = d(α − β log d), which turns over more slowly.
  • Best-of-n optimises the sample; reinforcement learning optimises the policy, and the two behave differently.

Practice

*Q. Which functional form does the overoptimisation paper fit for best-of-n? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ R(d) = d(α − β d)
  • R(d) = d(α − β log d)
  • R(d) = α e^(−β d)
  • R(d) = α d² + β

Correct.

Why: Best-of-n: a downward parabola through the origin, R(d) = d(α − βd). Reinforcement learning: R(d) = d(α − β log d), which turns over more slowly because the policy moves rather than the sample.

*Q. In the overoptimisation paper’s functional forms, what shape does best-of-n’s reward take as a function of the sample count d? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • Exponential growth that saturates
  • ✓ A downward parabola through the origin: R(d) = d(α − β d)
  • A straight line with slope α
  • A step function at the gold answer

Correct — rising at first, then falling as the proxy reward diverges from the true one.

Why: For best-of-n: R(d) = d(α − β d), a downward parabola through the origin — the proxy reward rises, peaks, and falls as d grows. Fitting both functional forms in a controlled setting is how the paper reads the fit and compares RL against best-of-n on the same proxy.

Go and do it

Lesson 11. The operational lesson

Where to stop

Estimated study time: 18 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what the turning point tells an practitioner
  • Explain the role of the KL coefficient as the thing that sets the stopping point
  • Argue for reporting the distance travelled alongside the score

The ideas

  • The KL coefficient is the dial that decides how far the policy is allowed to travel.
  • The turning point is where the marginal proxy reward equals the marginal true reward.
  • A report that gives a score without the distance travelled cannot be compared with another one.

Practice

*Q. What does the turning point of the overoptimisation curve tell an practitioner? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ The distance at which the marginal proxy reward equals the marginal true reward
  • The point at which the reward model stops working
  • The number of training steps to stop at
  • That the KL penalty should be removed

Correct.

Why: It is the optimal stopping point for a fixed budget, and it is what the KL coefficient is set to reach. Past it, the run is spending compute to make the true outcome worse.

*Q. In operational terms, what does the KL coefficient decide? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • How fast the policy learns per step
  • ✓ How far the policy is allowed to travel — the dial that sets the stopping point
  • How many PPO epochs run per batch
  • How the advantage estimator is initialised

Correct — which is why the distance travelled belongs next to the score in every report.

Why: The KL coefficient is the dial that decides how far the policy is allowed to travel — and the operational lesson is to report the distance travelled alongside the score, because a score without its KL budget says nothing about what was bought or at what price.
