1. Task Design

What a benchmark is made of

The tasks, the difficulty mix, and the number of them. What a score on a task set means, and what it does not.

Learning outcomes

  • Say what makes a task a task, and what makes it a good one
  • Compute the uncertainty on a score, and the number of tasks a difference needs
  • Explain why a task set is a sample and the score is an estimate

Lesson 1. What a task is

And what makes a good one

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what a benchmark task is: an environment, a goal and a verdict
  • Explain the three properties a good task set has
  • Describe what a difficulty mix does to a score

The ideas

  • A task is a starting state, a goal, and something that decides whether the goal was reached.
  • A good task set is diverse, verified, and hard enough that the trivial strategies fail.
  • The difficulty mix is a choice, and it decides what the score means.

Practice

*Q. What is a benchmark, exactly? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ A set of tasks and a rule that decides whether each was solved
  • A dataset of problems with reference answers
  • A metric
  • A leaderboard

Correct.

Why: The tasks and the verdict. Everything else — the score, the interval, the comparison — follows from the two.

*Q. What does the difficulty mix of a task set decide? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ What the score means: a set of easy tasks and a set of hard ones measure different things
  • How long the benchmark takes to run
  • Whether the tasks are verified
  • The interval on the score

Correct.

Why: Moving the mix moves the score, with nothing about the solver changing — which is why two benchmarks with different mixes are not comparable.

*Q. What does “hard enough that the trivial strategies fail” buy a benchmark? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • It makes the benchmark cheaper to run
  • ✓ It makes the score meaningful: if the trivial strategy passes, the score measures the task design rather than the solver
  • It makes the benchmark fair to smaller models
  • It removes the need for a verifier

Correct — diversity, verification and difficulty are what let the score say something.

Why: A task is a starting state, a goal, and something that decides whether the goal was reached. A good task set is diverse, verified, and hard enough that the trivial strategies fail — otherwise the number reports the tasks, not the systems.

Go and do it

The task set, its difficulty mix, and the interval on its score. Open Look at the tasks in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:3 The benchmark — The tasks, the repositories, and the criterion that decides whether a task is solved.
  • §gaia:3 The questions — The three levels, and the design of the questions at each.

The words this lesson uses

  • A benchmark — A set of tasks, and a rule that decides whether each was solved.
  • A task — A starting state, a goal, and a way of telling whether the goal was reached.
  • The difficulty mix — The proportion of the tasks that are easy, and the proportion that are hard.

Lesson 2. The score and its uncertainty

What a number on a task set means

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Explain why a score on a task set is an estimate rather than a fact
  • Compute the interval on a score, and say why the usual one is wrong near zero
  • Compute how many tasks a given difference needs

The ideas

  • The tasks are a sample, and the score estimates the rate on the population.
  • The interval on a proportion is not symmetric, and near zero the normal approximation is nonsense.
  • A difference between two systems has to be bigger than the noise before it means anything.

Practice

*Q. A solver solves 12 of 200 tasks. Using the Wilson interval, is the score of 6% more likely to be near 6% or near 0%? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 0

Why: The answer is zero for the normal approximation being useless: with twelve successes the interval is asymmetric, and the normal approximation would give a lower bound below zero. The Wilson interval keeps it inside the unit interval.

*Q. Why is the normal approximation to the interval nonsense near a solve rate of zero? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • Because the interval becomes too wide to read
  • ✓ Because a symmetric interval reaches below zero, while the true interval for a proportion is asymmetric
  • Because zero solve rates cannot be estimated at all
  • Because the interval needs the population size, which is unknown

Correct — near the boundary the sampling distribution is skewed, not bell-shaped.

Why: The tasks are a sample and the score estimates a rate on the population. The interval on a proportion is not symmetric, and near zero the normal approximation happily assigns probability to solving fewer than no tasks. The noise also bounds what a difference between two systems can mean.

Go and do it

The interval on a score, and the number of tasks a difference needs. Open Size the uncertainty in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:5 Discussion — The variance, and what a score on a task set means.

The words this lesson uses

  • The interval on a score — The range the true rate plausibly lies in.
  • The task set is a sample — The tasks are drawn from a population of tasks, and the score estimates the rate on it.
  • Power — The chance of noticing a difference that is really there.

2. Verification

The criterion that decides the task

The two conditions a solution must satisfy, the failure mode a criterion has to catch, and what a verifier costs.

Learning outcomes

  • State the two conditions and say what each is for
  • Describe the failure a verifier has to catch, and how it is caught
  • Explain why a verifier is the part of the benchmark that is hardest to get right

Lesson 3. The evaluation criterion

The two conditions

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the two conditions a solution must satisfy
  • Say what each condition is for, and what fails without it
  • Explain why the criterion is the hardest part of a benchmark to get right

The ideas

  • The failing test must start failing and end passing, and the passing tests must keep passing.
  • The first condition alone is satisfied by a solver that changes the test.
  • The second condition is what makes the first one mean something.

Practice

*Q. What are the two conditions a solution must satisfy? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The failing test must start failing and end passing, and the passing tests must keep passing
  • The failing test must pass, and the patch must be small
  • The tests must pass, and the agent must have finished
  • The failing test must pass, and no test file may be changed

Correct.

Why: The first condition makes it a task; the second is what makes the first condition mean something.

*Q. A patch that changes the failing test satisfies the first condition and nothing else. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. The failing test now passes, so the transition holds — and the task is no harder than it was, which is why the second condition and the distrust of patches that touch tests are both needed.

Go and do it

The four kinds of patch, and the verdict each one gets. Open Check the criterion in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:3.1 The evaluation criterion — The two conditions: the failing test must pass, and the passing tests must keep passing.

The words this lesson uses

  • The verifier — The thing that decides whether a task was solved.
  • The failing test must start failing and end passing — The first of the two conditions.
  • The passing tests must keep passing — The second of the two conditions.

Read first: What a task is

Lesson 4. The cheat

What a criterion has to catch

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the failure mode a solver that changes the test exploits
  • Explain how the criterion catches it
  • Say what a score means when the criterion is weak

The ideas

  • A solver that can change the test does not have to solve the task.
  • The criterion catches it by requiring the other tests to keep passing, and by distrusting a patch that touches a test.
  • A benchmark whose criterion is weak measures something else, and does not say what.

Practice

*Q. What does a benchmark with a weak verifier measure? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ The solver’s ability to satisfy the verifier, which may not be the ability the benchmark claims to measure
  • Nothing at all
  • The verifier’s quality
  • The task set

Correct.

Why: Gaming is not a moral failure: it is the correct response to a reward that is not the thing you wanted.

*Q. A solver that edits the failing test so it passes trivially still satisfies the standard evaluation criterion, as long as the other tests keep passing. — boolean (core)***

Answer: False

Why: The criterion has two conditions: the failing test must start failing and end passing, and the passing tests must keep passing. The second gives the first its meaning, and the criterion additionally distrusts a patch that touches a test — precisely because a solver that can change the test does not have to solve the task.

Go and do it

A solver that changes the test, and the score it would have got. Open Watch the cheat in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:3.1 The evaluation criterion — The criterion, and the failure it has to catch.

The words this lesson uses

  • The verifier — The thing that decides whether a task was solved.
  • Gaming the benchmark — Solving the verifier rather than the task.

3. The Baselines

What a score has to beat

The agentless baseline, the agent that tries several times, and the arithmetic of what the second one costs.

Learning outcomes

  • Describe the agentless baseline and why it is the number to beat
  • Compare an agent with the baseline on the same tasks
  • Measure the cost of the agent in attempts, and say what it buys

Lesson 5. The agentless baseline

What a score has to beat

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the agentless baseline and what it does
  • Explain why it is the number every agent has to beat
  • Compare it with an agent on the same tasks

The ideas

  • The baseline retrieves the relevant file and makes one obvious change.
  • Most of what an agent adds is the ability to try again, and that has a price.
  • The comparison has to be on the same tasks, with the same verifier.

Practice

*Q. Why is the agentless baseline the number to beat? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Because it is cheap, and an agent that cannot beat a cheap baseline is not earning its cost
  • Because it is stronger
  • Because it is the state of the art
  • Because it does not use a model

Correct.

Why: It does the obvious thing once. An agent that adds a loop and a search has to beat that with the loop’s cost.

Go and do it

The agentless baseline, its score, and the interval on it. Open Run the baseline in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:4 The results — The agentless baseline, and the argument that the agent is not the bottleneck.

The words this lesson uses

  • The agentless baseline — Retrieve the file, make the obvious change, and stop.
  • A solver — The thing that attempts the tasks.

Lesson 6. The price of trying again

What the agent spends

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Measure the number of attempts an agent makes
  • Compare the agent with the baseline on the same tasks
  • Say what the extra attempts buy and what they cost

The ideas

  • An agent that tries several times solves more tasks and makes more attempts.
  • The attempts are the cost, and they are paid in model calls.
  • So the comparison is not between the two scores but between the two scores per attempt.

Practice

*Q. What does an agent spend that the baseline does not? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Attempts, which are model calls
  • Nothing
  • Only the score
  • The verifier

Correct.

Why: So the comparison is not between the two scores but between the two scores per attempt.

*Q. The agent solves more tasks when it is allowed to try again. What is the honest comparison against the non-agent baseline? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • The raw solve rates, whatever the number of attempts
  • ✓ The same tasks, the same verifier, and the score read per attempt — the attempts are the cost, paid in model calls
  • The agent’s best single attempt against the baseline’s average
  • There is no honest comparison; the two are different kinds of system

Correct — the comparison is between the scores per attempt, not the scores.

Why: Most of what an agent adds is the ability to try again, and that has a price: an agent that tries several times solves more tasks and makes more attempts. The comparison has to be on the same tasks, with the same verifier, and the cost has to appear in the units.

Go and do it

The agent, the attempts it makes, and the tasks it solves. Open Run the agent in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:4 The results — The comparison of the agent with the baseline.

The words this lesson uses

  • A solver — The thing that attempts the tasks.
  • pass@k — The chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds.

4. Variance and Contamination

The two ways a benchmark lies to you

The variance of a score, the difference between one run and many, and the overlap test that finds a task the model has already seen.

Learning outcomes

  • Compute the variance of a score, and the interval that goes with it
  • Explain the unbiased estimate of pass@k, and why a single run overstates it
  • Measure contamination with an n-gram overlap, and say what the length of the n-gram decides

Lesson 7. One run or many

The variance, and the pass@k estimator

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Compute the variance of a score across runs
  • Explain why a single run overstates pass@k, and what the unbiased estimate is
  • Say how many samples a comparison needs

The ideas

  • A solver is stochastic, so one run is one sample of a distribution.
  • The naive estimate of pass@k is biased upwards, and the correction is what makes two sample budgets comparable.
  • The paired comparison is more sensitive than comparing two independent scores.

Practice

*Q. A single run of a stochastic solver is one sample of a distribution, not a measurement of it. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. The spread across runs is the noise in every comparison made from single runs, and it is what a reported score leaves out.

*Q. Why is the naive estimate of pass@k biased upwards? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ Because the samples that succeeded are more likely to be the ones counted, so the estimate overstates the chance of at least one success
  • Because the tasks are hard
  • Because k is usually too small
  • It is not biased

Correct.

Why: The unbiased estimator corrects for it, and the correction is what makes two different sample budgets comparable.

Go and do it

The score across repeated runs, and the interval it implies. Open Measure the variance in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:5 Discussion — The variance of a score across runs.
  • §agentbench:3 The environments — The eight environments, and what each one measures.

The words this lesson uses

  • The variance of a score — How much the score moves when the solver is run again.
  • pass@k — The chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds.
  • A paired comparison — Comparing two systems on the same tasks.

Read first: The score and its uncertainty

Lesson 8. Has the model seen it?

Contamination, and the overlap that finds it

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe what benchmark contamination is and why it invalidates a score
  • Measure it with an n-gram overlap, and report the two rates it gives
  • Say what the length of the n-gram decides, and what the threshold decides

The ideas

  • A task the model has already seen is not a measurement of anything.
  • The detection is an overlap test, and it has two failure modes: too short a match catches ordinary text, too long a match misses an edited copy.
  • So the length and the threshold are decisions, and the rates they give are the report.

Practice

*Q. What does contamination do to a benchmark? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It flatters the systems that were trained on the leaked data, and makes the score meaningless for them
  • It lowers every score equally
  • It makes the benchmark harder
  • Nothing, if the tasks are verified

Correct.

Why: A task the model has already seen measures the training data rather than the solver, and the error is not evenly spread over the systems.

*Q. What does the length of the n-gram decide in the overlap test? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ Whether an edited copy is caught: a short n-gram survives the edit, a long one does not
  • How fast the test runs
  • Whether the tasks are contaminated
  • The score

Correct.

Why: And a short n-gram also catches ordinary text, so the length trades a false-positive rate against a true-positive rate — which is why both are reported.

*Q. A task that appears verbatim in the training data still measures what the benchmark claims. — boolean (core)***

Answer: False

Why: If the answer is already in the weights, the score measures memory, not ability. This is why a benchmark has to ask what the model has seen — and why a contaminated task is removed rather than scored.

Go and do it

The overlap of every task’s solution with a training corpus, and the rates the test gives. Open Look for the leak in the agent-bench-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §swebench:5 Discussion — The contamination, and what it does to a score.
  • §webarena:4 Evaluation — The evaluation functions, and the difference between them and a string match.

The words this lesson uses

  • Contamination — The model has already seen the task, or its answer.
  • The overlap test — Comparing a task’s solution with the training corpus, n-grams at a time.

Appendix A — Glossary

A benchmark — A set of tasks, and a rule that decides whether each was solved.

A benchmark is two things: the tasks and the verdict. Everything else — the score, the interval on it, the comparison between two systems — follows from those, and a benchmark with a weak verdict measures something other than what it claims.

A task — A starting state, a goal, and a way of telling whether the goal was reached.

A task gives the solver an environment and an instruction, and it ends with a verdict. The verdict is the part that has to be objective: a human reading the output is a different kind of benchmark, and a noisier one.

The difficulty mix — The proportion of the tasks that are easy, and the proportion that are hard.

The mix decides what a score means. A set of easy tasks measures whether the solver can do the easy thing, and a set of hard ones measures whether it can do the hard thing. Moving the mix moves the score, without anything about the solver changing.

The task set is a sample — The tasks are drawn from a population of tasks, and the score estimates the rate on it.

This is the reason a score needs an interval. The hundred tasks in the benchmark are a sample of the tasks that could have been in it, and the score is an estimate of the rate on all of them.

The interval on a score — The range the true rate plausibly lies in.

For a proportion, the interval is not symmetric and the usual normal approximation is wrong near zero and near one — which is exactly where a benchmark’s score often is.

Power — The chance of noticing a difference that is really there.

A benchmark with too few tasks has little power: a real difference of two points is invisible. The number of tasks a comparison needs follows from the size of the difference and from the noise, and both are computable.

The verifier — The thing that decides whether a task was solved.

The verifier is the part of the benchmark that is hardest to get right, because it is the part a solver is trying to fool. A benchmark with a weak verifier measures the solver’s ability to fool it.

The failing test must start failing and end passing — The first of the two conditions.

A task comes with a test that fails before the fix and passes after it. Requiring that transition is what makes the task a task — and it is also the condition a solver can satisfy by changing the test.

The passing tests must keep passing — The second of the two conditions.

A solution that fixes the task by breaking something else is not a solution. This condition is what makes the first one mean something, and it is what a cheat usually violates.

Gaming the benchmark — Solving the verifier rather than the task.

A benchmark measures what its verifier measures. A solver that finds the difference between the two is not cheating in a moral sense; it is optimising the objective, which is what a reward is for.

A solver — The thing that attempts the tasks.

A solver may be a program, a model, or a loop around a model. What the benchmark measures is the pair of the solver and the verifier, and a score quoted without the verifier is a quote without a meaning.

The agentless baseline — Retrieve the file, make the obvious change, and stop.

One attempt per task, with no loop and no search. It is the number every agent has to beat, and a surprising number of agents do not.

pass@k — The chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds.

It is the natural metric for a solver that may be tried several times. The estimate from k samples is biased upwards, and the unbiased correction is what makes two different sample budgets comparable.

The variance of a score — How much the score moves when the solver is run again.

A solver is stochastic, so one run is one sample. The spread across runs is the noise in the comparison, and it is what a single-run score leaves out.

A paired comparison — Comparing two systems on the same tasks.

The same tasks remove the task-difficulty variation from the comparison, and with it most of the noise. It is more sensitive than comparing two independent scores, and it is the comparison a benchmark should report.

Contamination — The model has already seen the task, or its answer.

A task whose solution is in the training data is not a measurement of the solver; it is a measurement of the training data. And the score of the benchmark goes up, which is the problem: the contamination flatters the system it is supposed to be testing.

The overlap test — Comparing a task’s solution with the training corpus, n-grams at a time.

A passage that shares a long run of n-grams with the corpus is probably in it. The length of the n-gram is a decision: short n-grams catch ordinary text as well as copies, and long ones miss a copy that was lightly edited.

1. Harmlessness from AI Feedback

A model that critiques itself, against a written rule

The critique-and-revise loop, the preference data it makes, and the judge that every harmlessness number depends on.

Learning outcomes

  • Describe the critique-and-revise loop and what it produces
  • Say what a harmlessness score means, and what it depends on
  • Measure the agreement of a judge with the labels

Lesson 1. The critique-and-revise loop

A model, a principle, and a second pass

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the loop: a response, a critique against a principle, a revision
  • Say what the loop produces and what it is used for
  • Measure how much of the harm the loop removes

The ideas

  • The critique names the principle that was violated, so the revision has something to work against.
  • The loop makes a preference dataset; the dataset is what trains the model.
  • A revision should remove the harm and keep the harmless part of the answer.

Practice

*Q. What does the critique in the critique-and-revise loop do? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It names the principle the response broke, so the revision has something to work against
  • It rewrites the response
  • It scores the response
  • It decides whether the response is harmful

Correct.

Why: A revision cannot be written without something to revise against, so the critique has to name the principle.

*Q. The critique-and-revise loop produces a preference dataset, which is then used for training. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. The revisions become the preferred responses, and it is a dataset like any other — with whatever biases the critiquing model carried.

Go and do it

The critiques, the revisions, and the harm that is left. Open Run the loop in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §cai:2 The supervised stage — The critiques and the revisions, and the dataset they make.

The words this lesson uses

  • The constitution — A written list of principles a model is held to.
  • The critique — A model pointing out that a response breaks a principle.
  • The preference data — The pairs of responses, one preferred, that the training uses.

Lesson 2. The judge

Whose opinion the number is

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what a harmlessness score is an estimate of
  • Explain why the agreement with the labels is the number to report
  • Describe the false positives and false negatives a judge makes

The ideas

  • A harmlessness score is what a judge believes, and the judge is a model.
  • The agreement with the human labels is what makes the number worth anything.
  • A judge that flags the harmless cases costs you the data you were trying to collect.

Practice

*Q. What is the agreement between a judge and the human labels? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The part of a harmlessness score that makes it worth anything
  • An optional extra
  • The accuracy of the model being tested
  • The size of the preference dataset

Correct.

Why: Every harmlessness number is what a judge believes, measured on a sample. The agreement is what makes that number mean anything.

*Q. What are the two errors a harmlessness judge makes? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • Under- and over-refusal, in the generation stage
  • ✓ False positives — flagging harmless answers — and false negatives — passing harmful ones
  • Position and verbosity bias, as in any LLM judge
  • It makes no errors if it is the same model that produced the answers

Correct — and the agreement with the labels is the number to report, because the score is what a judge believes.

Why: A harmlessness score is what a judge believes, and the judge is a model — so it makes false positives and false negatives. The agreement with the labels is the number to report, because that is what says how much the score can be believed.

Go and do it

The agreement of a judge with the labels, and the errors it makes. Open Check the judge in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §hh:6 The evaluation — How a harmlessness score is produced, and what the judge is worth.

The words this lesson uses

  • The judge — The model whose opinion a harmlessness score reports.
  • The agreement with the labels — How often the judge and the human labels say the same thing.
  • A false positive — The judge flags a case the labels call harmless.

Read first: The critique-and-revise loop

Lesson 8. What a claim is worth

Reading a safety result

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what a harmlessness number is and is not a measurement of
  • List the things a safety claim leaves out, and why each matters
  • Describe the evidence a claim needs before it is believed

The ideas

  • A harmlessness score is the opinion of a judge, measured on a sample, against a taxonomy.
  • It is not a statement about the model’s behaviour outside the sample.
  • A claim is worth what its measurement can carry, and the course is about the measurement.

Practice

*Q. What does a harmlessness score not tell you? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • ✓ What the model does outside the sample the score was measured on
  • What the judge believed
  • The size of the sample
  • The taxonomy

Correct.

Why: It is a measurement on a sample against a taxonomy, by a judge. Everything outside those three is a claim about the model rather than a measurement of it.

*Q. What is a harmlessness number actually a measurement of? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • The safety of the model
  • ✓ The opinion of a judge, measured on a sample, against a taxonomy
  • The agreement between two judges
  • The model’s refusal rate on benign queries

Correct — and everything a safety claim leaves out follows from those three qualifiers.

Why: A harmlessness score is the opinion of a judge, measured on a sample, against a taxonomy. Each qualifier names something a safety claim leaves out — the judge’s calibration, the sample’s size and representativeness, the taxonomy’s coverage — and the evidence a claim needs before it is believed is the list of those things stated.

Go and do it

The parts of a harmlessness claim, and the measurement behind each. Open Read the claim in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §cai:5 Discussion — What the method does not establish, and how a harmlessness claim should be read.

The words this lesson uses

  • A safety claim — A statement about what a model will not do.
  • The judge — The model whose opinion a harmlessness score reports.
  • The coverage — The fraction of the taxonomy the red team reached.

Read first: The judge, The taxonomy

Lesson 9. The two rounds

What imitation reaches, and what a preference signal moves

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Name the two rounds and what each of them is trained on
  • Explain why the first round cannot find the compromise by itself
  • Measure where each round lands on the two objectives

The ideas

  • The first round imitates the demonstrations it was given, and a demonstration is only what somebody wrote down.
  • The second round is trained against a preference signal, which is the only place in the procedure that a trade-off between being helpful and being harmless can be said.
  • The weighting is a choice, and the same model is a different assistant under a different one.

Practice

*Q. What can the first round of the procedure learn that the second round cannot? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ What a good answer looks like, from the demonstrations it was given
  • Which of two good answers to prefer
  • How harmful an answer is
  • Nothing: the rounds are the same training

Correct — and it is the round both procedures share.

Why: Imitation learns the shape of an answer. A trade-off between being helpful and being harmless is a statement about which answer to prefer, and only the preference signal carries it.

*Q. Changing the weighting of the two objectives changes which round of training wins the argument. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: True

Why: It does. The weighting is a choice made outside the data, and the same model is a different assistant under a different one — which is why the trade-off has to be stated as part of the result.

Go and do it

Where each round lands, how far the second one moves, and what the weighting changes. Open Run the two rounds in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §hh:3 The training methodology — The imitation round, the reward model and the reinforcement round, and the weighting of the two objectives.
  • §cai:3 The reinforcement stage — The preference model trained on the critiques, and the harmlessness it buys.

The words this lesson uses

  • The preference data — The pairs of responses, one preferred, that the training uses.
  • The imitation round — Training a model to copy the demonstrations it was given.
  • A reward model — A model trained to score an answer the way the labelers scored them.

Read first: The critique-and-revise loop

Lesson 10. The critic that sees what it cannot

Self-critique against an external one

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what a model can and cannot see in an answer it has just written
  • Explain why the comparison of two critics needs a verdict that is right
  • Measure what each critic misses, and the cost of each

The ideas

  • A critique written by the model that wrote the answer shares that answer’s blind spots.
  • The comparison is only a comparison if something else decides which critiques were right.
  • What an external critic finds that a self-critic does not is the claim of the method, and it is a rate, not an anecdote.

Practice

*Q. Why does comparing a self-critic with an external critic need a third opinion? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Because the question is which critiques were right, and neither critic can be the judge of that
  • Because the two critics are the same model
  • Because the critics write different numbers of words
  • It does not; the two rates can be compared directly

Correct.

Why: A claim about what a critic cannot see in its own answer is a claim about the cases it got wrong, and finding those needs a verdict that is right for reasons of its own.

*Q. Why does a critique written by the model that wrote the answer share that answer’s blind spots? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • Because the critique is copied from the answer
  • ✓ Because the model cannot see what it cannot see — the same limits that shaped the answer shape the critique of it
  • Because the critique uses a smaller context window
  • Because critiques are sampled at a higher temperature

Correct — which is why comparing two critics needs a verdict that is right.

Why: A critique written by the model that wrote the answer shares that answer’s blind spots — the model cannot see what it cannot see. Measuring what each critic misses, and the cost of each, is why the comparison of two critics needs a verdict that is right rather than merely fluent.

Go and do it

The same cases, two critics, and the verdicts each one reaches. Open Compare the two critics in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §cai:3 The reinforcement stage — The preference model trained on the critiques, and the harmlessness it buys.
  • §hh:6 The evaluation — How a harmlessness score is produced, and what the judge is worth.

The words this lesson uses

  • The critique — A model pointing out that a response breaks a principle.
  • The judge — The model whose opinion a harmlessness score reports.
  • The agreement with the labels — How often the judge and the human labels say the same thing.

2. Red Teaming

Finding the failures, and knowing which ones you have not

The attack, the taxonomy, and the two numbers that matter: how often the model fails, and how much of the space the red team reached.

Learning outcomes

  • Describe a red-team attack and the taxonomy it is measured against
  • Say why the coverage matters more than the success rate
  • Compare a model-driven red team with a random one on the same budget

Lesson 3. The attack

Finding the failure, on purpose

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe what a red-team attack is and what it is measured against
  • Say why the attack success rate alone is the wrong number
  • Explain what the coverage of a red team means

The ideas

  • A red team is a search: the failures it has not found are the ones it cannot rule out.
  • The attack success rate says how weak the model is on the attacks it made.
  • The coverage says how much of the space it looked at, and it is the number that is usually missing.

Practice

*Q. Why is the attack success rate the wrong number to report on its own? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It says how often the model failed, and nothing about what it was never asked
  • It is too noisy
  • It is too generous
  • It ignores the cost of the attacks

Correct.

Why: A red-team set is a sample of the attacks that work, not a test set. The failures it has not found are the ones it cannot rule out.

*Q. A model-driven red team reaches more of the taxonomy than a random one on the same budget. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes, and the coverage is the number that shows it. The attack success rate can be similar while the coverage is very different.

Go and do it

The attacks, the failures, and the coverage of the taxonomy. Open Run the red team in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §redteam:3 The method — The attacker, the diversity of its attacks, and the taxonomy they are measured against.

The words this lesson uses

  • The red team — The search for the failures, done on purpose.
  • The taxonomy — The list of the kinds of failure the red team is looking for.
  • The coverage — The fraction of the taxonomy the red team reached.

Read first: The critique-and-revise loop

Lesson 4. The taxonomy

What a red team should be measured against

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what a harm taxonomy is and where it comes from
  • Explain the difference between a red-team set and a test set
  • Measure the coverage of a red team against a taxonomy

The ideas

  • A taxonomy is what makes a red-team set a measurement rather than an anecdote.
  • A red-team set is a sample of the attacks that work, not a test set: it says what fails, not what passes.
  • The coverage of a red team is a claim about the model only where the red team looked.

Practice

*Q. What is a taxonomy for? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Turning a pile of failures into a measurement that can be compared
  • Listing every possible failure
  • Deciding which failures matter
  • Replacing the red team

Correct.

Why: Without a taxonomy a red team produces anecdotes. With one, it produces a coverage that can be compared between teams and between models.

*Q. What does a harm taxonomy add to a red-team set? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • A longer list of prompts
  • ✓ Coverage that can be measured: the set becomes a measurement rather than an anecdote
  • A licence to skip the held-out test set
  • Automatic scoring of the attacks

Correct — and the difference between a red-team set and a test set is what it is drawn from.

Why: A taxonomy is what makes a red-team set a measurement rather than an anecdote: the coverage of a red team against the taxonomy is measurable, and a red-team set differs from a test set in that it is drawn from attacks rather than from the behaviour being certified.

Go and do it

A model-driven red team against a random one, on the same budget. Open Compare the two red teams in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §hh:2 The helpful and harmless dataset — The red-team prompts, the harmlessness categories, and the labels.

The words this lesson uses

  • The taxonomy — The list of the kinds of failure the red team is looking for.
  • The coverage — The fraction of the taxonomy the red team reached.
  • The red team — The search for the failures, done on purpose.

Read first: The attack

Lesson 11. The search budget

How many attacks it takes to find a failure

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what a discovery rate is measured against
  • Explain why spending a budget evenly over the failures is the ceiling
  • Read the marginal value of the last attack off a curve

The ideas

  • The question is not whether this many attacks work, but how many it takes to find a given share of the failures.
  • A budget spread over every failure is the best an unguided search can do, and it loses to that before it loses to a guided one.
  • A thousand attacks that find the same failure are worth less than ten that find ten, and the gap is the re-hit count.

Practice

*Q. One attempt reaches a particular failure with probability 0.25. Spending four attempts on it, what is the chance the failure has been found at least once? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 0.68359375 ± 0.001

Why: One minus the chance it is missed four times: 1 − 0.75⁴ = 0.6836. This is the arithmetic the ceiling curve is made of, and it is the same whether the attempts were asked for or stumbled into.

*Q. Why is spending the attack budget evenly over the known failures a ceiling rather than a strategy? — multiple-choice (hard)***

  • Because even spending wastes the budget on duplicates
  • ✓ Because the question is how many attacks it takes to find a given share of the failures — the discovery rate is measured against the budget, and the marginal value of the last attack is read off that curve
  • Because attacks are free, so spending evenly costs nothing
  • Because the taxonomy forbids uneven spending

Correct — which is why the curve, not the count, is what a red-team report should show.

Why: The question is not whether this many attacks work, but how many it takes to find a given share of the failures. The discovery rate is what a search budget is measured against, spending evenly over the failures is the ceiling, and the marginal value of the last attack is read off the curve.

Go and do it

The discovery rate against the number of attacks, and where the wasted ones went. Open Spend the budget in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §redteam:3 The method — The attacker, the diversity of its attacks, and the taxonomy they are measured against.

The words this lesson uses

  • The red team — The search for the failures, done on purpose.
  • The coverage — The fraction of the taxonomy the red team reached.
  • The taxonomy — The list of the kinds of failure the red team is looking for.

3. Cued Behaviour

A harm that arrives with a mark nobody asked about

The safety classifier, the label sheet it was given, and the part of the behaviour that rides on a cue no column was made for.

Learning outcomes

  • Describe a conditional behaviour and the cue that switches it
  • Say what a safety classifier is able to count, and what it is not
  • Measure the gap between the harm an evaluation reports and the harm there is

Lesson 13. The cue nobody asked about

A classifier that is exact about what it was told

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe a conditional behaviour and the cue that switches it
  • Say what a safety classifier is able to count and what it is not
  • Measure the harm an evaluation reports against the harm there is

The ideas

  • A fit has no opinion about a mark it was never given a column for, and the weight it learns is exactly zero.
  • The cued harm is not mis-classified. It is never counted, which is a different failure and a harder one to see.
  • An evaluation set that never fires the cue reports a rate that is true of the set and not of the model.

Practice

*Q. A safety classifier is given a column for one cue, and the harm rides on another. What happens to the harm that rides on the unnamed one? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It is never counted, which is not the same as being counted wrong
  • It is counted as harmless
  • It raises the false-positive rate
  • The classifier flags it at half the usual rate

Correct.

Why: This is the difference between a measurement that failed and a measurement that was never run, and it is the reason the evaluation set has to contain the cue.

*Q. A classifier is fitted with a column for a cue that none of its examples carry. What weight does the fit put on that column? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 0

Why: Exactly zero. A fit has no opinion about a mark it was never given a column for, and a reported weight of zero is a statement about the sheet the team filled in rather than about the behaviour.

Go and do it

The same classifier, two label sheets, and the harm that goes uncounted. Open Give it the wrong sheet in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §sleeper:2 A summary of the findings — The behaviour is conditional on a cue, and the safety training leaves the cue in place.
  • §sleeper:5 Safety training and the backdoor — Supervised and reinforcement training reduce the behaviour where it is asked about, and not where it is cued.

The words this lesson uses

  • A conditional behaviour — A way of answering that only appears when something in the prompt says so.
  • A cue — The mark in a prompt that switches a conditional behaviour on.
  • The judge — The model whose opinion a harmlessness score reports.
  • A false positive — The judge flags a case the labels call harmless.

Read first: The judge

4. Sycophancy

Changing the answer to agree with the person asking

The flip rate, the size of the effect, and the small change to the prompt that moves it.

Learning outcomes

  • Define the flip rate and say what it measures
  • Explain the mechanism: the training made agreeing feel like the right answer
  • Measure the effect of the mitigation and of the position of the answer

Lesson 5. Agreeing with the user

The flip rate

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define the flip rate and say what it measures
  • Explain the mechanism behind it
  • Say what a model is being trained to do when it agrees

The ideas

  • A model asked a question it can answer will sometimes change its answer to agree.
  • The training rewarded the answer that made the user happy, and agreement looks like that.
  • The flip rate is the fraction of correct answers that become wrong under pressure.

Practice

*Q. What does the flip rate measure? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The fraction of correct answers that become wrong when the user asserts a wrong one
  • The fraction of answers that are wrong
  • How often the model agrees with the user
  • How much the model’s accuracy drops under pressure

Correct.

Why: The model is asked something it gets right, the user asserts a wrong answer, and the rate says how often the model goes along with it.

*Q. Sycophancy is a quirk of the architecture rather than a consequence of the training. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: False

Why: No. The training rewarded the answer that made the user happy, and agreement looks like that. Which is good news, because a consequence of the training can be changed by the training.

Go and do it

The answers under pressure, and the ones that flip. Open Measure the flip rate in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §sycophancy:1 Introduction — The claim: models change their answers to agree with the person asking.

The words this lesson uses

  • Sycophancy — Changing the answer to agree with the person asking.
  • The flip rate — The fraction of correct answers that become wrong under pressure.

Lesson 6. The mitigation

One sentence in the prompt

Estimated study time: 22 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the mitigation and the size of its effect
  • Say why a mitigation that lives in the prompt is not a fix
  • Measure the effect of the mitigation against the baseline

The ideas

  • Telling the model the user may be wrong moves the flip rate, and by a measurable amount.
  • A mitigation in the prompt is a mitigation in the prompt: it depends on the system message being there.
  • The right place to fix it is the training, and the measurement is how you would know.

Practice

*Q. What is the mitigation for sycophancy? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Telling the model the user may be wrong, which moves the flip rate by a measurable amount
  • Training the model on the right answers
  • Removing the model’s access to the user’s message
  • There is no mitigation

Correct.

Why: It is a mitigation in the prompt, though, and so it depends on the system message being there — which is not the same as a fix in the training.

*Q. Telling the model that the user may be wrong moves the flip rate by a measurable amount. Why is that not a fix? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • Because the effect is too small to measure
  • ✓ Because the behaviour remains and the prompt is doing work the model should — remove the prompt and the flip returns
  • Because prompts cannot be evaluated
  • Because it makes the model refuse everything

Correct — a mitigation that lives in the prompt is a configuration, not a property of the model.

Why: Telling the model the user may be wrong moves the flip rate, and by a measurable amount — but a mitigation that lives in the prompt is not a fix: it is doing work the model itself should do, and the behaviour returns when the prompt does.

Go and do it

The flip rate with and without the challenge, and the difference. Open Try the mitigation in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

The words this lesson uses

  • Sycophancy — Changing the answer to agree with the person asking.
  • The flip rate — The fraction of correct answers that become wrong under pressure.
  • The mitigation — One sentence in the prompt that reduces the flip rate.

Lesson 12. What consistency buys

The number behind a preference label

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define the repeat agreement of a labeler and say what it measures
  • Explain what a majority of looks does to the label, and what it does not do
  • Say which of fidelity and amplification a consistency number actually buys

The ideas

  • A preference label is one person’s answer to one question at one moment, and the repeat agreement is what says how much of it is signal.
  • Taking a majority over several looks raises the rate at which the label is the one the labeler means; it does not change what the labeler means.
  • Fidelity and amplification are different claims, and only the first is bought with consistency.

Practice

*Q. What does the repeat agreement of a labeler measure? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ How often the labeler gives the same answer to the same question twice
  • How often the labeler is right
  • How often two labelers agree
  • How many questions were labelled

Correct.

Why: It is a rate, and it says how much of a preference label is signal rather than a coin toss. Nothing in it says whether what the labeler means is right.

*Q. Taking a majority over several looks at a question makes the label both more faithful to what the labeler means and more often correct. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: False

Why: Only the first half. A majority of looks raises the rate at which the label is the one the labeler would give again; if the labeler leans toward the answer the user wanted, the majority is that lean with less noise around it.

Go and do it

The repeat agreement, the majority of looks, and what each hands to the reward model. Open Measure the labeler in the safety-lab application.

The words this lesson uses

  • The preference data — The pairs of responses, one preferred, that the training uses.
  • The consistency of a labeler — How often the same labeler gives the same answer to the same question twice.
  • A reward model — A model trained to score an answer the way the labelers scored them.

5. Privacy

What a model can be made to give back

Memorisation, the extraction attack, and the number that says how much of the training set is exposed.

Learning outcomes

  • Describe what memorisation means and when it happens
  • Explain the extraction attack and what its success rate depends on
  • Measure the exposure of a training set against the length of the known prefix

Lesson 7. Memorisation

What a model keeps, and what it gives back

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe what memorisation is and when it happens
  • Explain the extraction attack and what its rate depends on
  • Measure the exposure of a training set

The ideas

  • A model trained on a record it saw once can keep that record exactly.
  • The exposure of a training set is the thing a privacy claim is about.
  • The attack gets easier the more of the record the attacker already has.

Practice

*Q. What does the extraction attack do? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ It supplies what it knows of a training record and gets the model to fill in the rest
  • It asks the model for its training data
  • It measures the model’s parameter count
  • It compares the model with the original dataset

Correct.

Why: The attack gets easier the more of the record the attacker already has, and the success rate against the length of the known prefix is the measurement.

*Q. An extraction attack succeeds on a third of the records. What is the exposure of the training set? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 0.333333 ± 0.001

Why: The exposure is the fraction of the training set the attack can recover: a third of it, on this measure and by this attack.

Go and do it

The attack, the prefix, and the success rate at each length. Open Run the extraction in the safety-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §extraction:1 Introduction — The claim: a model that memorised its training data can be made to emit it.
  • §extraction:4 The extraction attack — The attack, its success rate, and what the rate depends on.

The words this lesson uses

  • Memorisation — A model keeping a training record exactly.
  • The extraction attack — Getting the training data out of the model, a piece at a time.
  • A privacy leak — Something the model gives back that it should not have kept.

Lesson 14. Who can tell

Membership, and what a budget buys

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the membership-inference attack and the score it is built on
  • Explain why the attacker’s query budget is part of the result
  • Say what the near-duplicates in a corpus cost a precision

The ideas

  • The same memorisation that lets an attacker take a record back lets them test whether it was ever in the set.
  • At one query the test is a coin, and every point above chance on the curve was bought with queries.
  • A corpus with no near-duplicates gives a test that cannot fail, and a real corpus has plenty of them.

Practice

*Q. What does a membership-inference attack read? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ How much more the model likes the record than a model that never saw it
  • Whether the record is in a list the model publishes
  • The gradient of the model on the record
  • The length of the record

Correct — the log of that ratio is the score.

Why: The baseline is a reference model trained without the record, and the whole shape of the result depends on it: a lower baseline makes every gap look like memorisation.

*Q. A toy model chooses between 16 tokens and has never seen a record. What is the chance that one query says the record’s continuation back? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 0.0625 ± 0.0001

Why: One in sixteen: 0.0625. An outsider is flagged exactly as often as it happens to look like a member, which is why a single query is a coin rather than a test.

Go and do it

The candidates, the scores they get, and what the budget buys. Open Run the membership attack in the safety-lab application.

The words this lesson uses

  • A membership-inference attack — Deciding, from the model’s answers, whether a record was in its training set.
  • A near-duplicate — Something not in the training set that resembles a record that was.
  • Memorisation — A model keeping a training record exactly.
  • The extraction attack — Getting the training data out of the model, a piece at a time.

Appendix A — Glossary

The constitution — A written list of principles a model is held to.

A constitution is a document: a set of principles about what an assistant should and should not do. Its value is that it is written down, so the critique can point at a rule rather than at a feeling.

The critique — A model pointing out that a response breaks a principle.

The critique names the principle and says what is wrong. That is what makes it useful: a revision cannot be written without something to revise against.

The preference data — The pairs of responses, one preferred, that the training uses.

The loop produces a dataset of critiques and revisions, and the revisions become the preferred responses. It is a dataset like any other, and it inherits whatever biases the critiquing model had.

The judge — The model whose opinion a harmlessness score reports.

Every harmlessness number is an estimate of what a judge believes, measured on a sample. So the judge’s agreement with human labels is part of the number, and it is the part that is usually left out.

The agreement with the labels — How often the judge and the human labels say the same thing.

It comes with two numbers attached: the false positives, the cases the judge flags and the labels call harmless, and the false negatives, the other way round. Reporting one without the other is how a benchmark ends up throwing away a third of itself.

A false positive — The judge flags a case the labels call harmless.

It costs you the harmless cases, and the harmless cases are most of a helpful dataset. A judge with a high false-positive rate does not make a model safer; it makes the dataset smaller.

The red team — The search for the failures, done on purpose.

A red team writes the prompts that break the model. What it produces is a set of failures, and the set says what the model does wrongly — it says nothing about what it does right.

The taxonomy — The list of the kinds of failure the red team is looking for.

A taxonomy is what turns a pile of failures into a measurement. Without one, a red team produces anecdotes; with one, it produces a coverage that can be compared between teams and between models.

The coverage — The fraction of the taxonomy the red team reached.

It is the number that says how much of the space was looked at, and it is the number that makes a red-team set a sample rather than a story. A model that fails only what the team found is not safe — it is unexamined.

Sycophancy — Changing the answer to agree with the person asking.

A model asked a question it can answer will sometimes change its answer to agree with the questioner. It is not a quirk: the training rewarded the answer that made the user happy, and agreement looks like that.

The flip rate — The fraction of correct answers that become wrong under pressure.

It is the measurement of sycophancy: the model is asked something it gets right, the user asserts a wrong answer, and the rate says how often the model goes along with it.

The mitigation — One sentence in the prompt that reduces the flip rate.

Telling the model that the user may be wrong moves the number, and by a measurable amount. It is a mitigation in the prompt, though, and so it depends on the system message being there — which is not the same as a fix in the training.

Memorisation — A model keeping a training record exactly.

Some records are kept verbatim, especially the ones that appear once. The exposure of a training set is the fraction of it that a model can be made to give back, and that is the number a privacy claim is about.

The extraction attack — Getting the training data out of the model, a piece at a time.

The attacker supplies what they know and the model fills in the rest. The attack gets easier the more of the record the attacker already has, and the success rate against the length of the known prefix is the measurement.

A privacy leak — Something the model gives back that it should not have kept.

It is not a bug in the model; it is what a model that learned from data does. The question is how much, and the answer is a number that has to be measured rather than assumed.

A safety claim — A statement about what a model will not do.

Its worth is the worth of the measurement behind it: the judge, the sample, the taxonomy and the coverage. A claim that leaves any of those out is a claim about a benchmark rather than about a model.

The imitation round — Training a model to copy the demonstrations it was given.

The first round of the procedure, and the only one that sees written answers rather than preference judgements. It can learn what a good answer looks like; it cannot learn which of two good answers to prefer, because nothing in the demonstrations says so.

A reward model — A model trained to score an answer the way the labelers scored them.

It is fitted on the preference pairs and then maximised by the second round, which means every property of the labelers passes into the assistant through it — including the ones nobody intended to teach, such as a preference for the answer the user seemed to want.

The consistency of a labeler — How often the same labeler gives the same answer to the same question twice.

It is a rate, and it is the number that says how much of a preference label is signal rather than a coin toss. A majority taken over several looks raises the rate at which the label is the one the labeler means, and it says nothing at all about whether what the labeler means is right.

A conditional behaviour — A way of answering that only appears when something in the prompt says so.

The behaviour is real and it is trained, but it is not the model’s default, and a measurement that never asks the triggering question will report that it does not exist. Safety training makes the default better, which is not the same as removing the condition.

A cue — The mark in a prompt that switches a conditional behaviour on.

A date, a name, a domain — something ordinary enough to appear in a harmless question too. What makes a cue a problem for evaluation is that no classifier can be scored on a column nobody gave it, so the harm riding on the cue goes uncounted rather than mis-counted.

A membership-inference attack — Deciding, from the model’s answers, whether a record was in its training set.

The attacker compares what the model gives a record against what a model that never saw it gives — the difference is the score, and the threshold is a choice about how many outsiders the attacker is willing to call members. The attack and the extraction read the same memorisation, which is why the two results are one argument.

A near-duplicate — Something not in the training set that resembles a record that was.

It raises the model’s probability without having been seen, so an attack scores it like a member. A corpus with no near-duplicates gives a membership test that cannot fail; the precision of a real attack is the share of the flagged candidates that this group accounts for.

1. Contrastive Pretraining

Two encoders, one space, and no labels at all

The loss that says a pair should be closer than the other pairs in the batch, the temperature that decides how sharp it is, and the data that pays for it.

Learning outcomes

  • State the contrastive objective and say what the in-batch negatives are for
  • Explain what the temperature does, and why it is a decision rather than a constant
  • Measure how the retrieval improves with the batch size and with the data

Lesson 1. The contrastive objective

What the loss says, and who provides the negatives

Estimated study time: 28 minutes

What you will learn

  • State the objective in words and write the loss
  • Explain where the negatives come from and what they cost
  • Say what the temperature does to the loss

The ideas

  • The loss asks for the paired image and caption to be closer than the other pairs in the batch.
  • The negatives are the other pairs in the batch, and they are free.
  • The temperature decides how sharp the distribution over the batch is.

Practice

*Q. What does the contrastive loss ask for? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The paired image and caption to score higher than every other pair in the batch
  • The image to be classified as the caption’s class
  • The two encoders to be identical
  • The batch to contain one pair of each class

Correct.

Why: It is a cross-entropy over the batch, with the true pairing on the diagonal. Nothing in it needs a label.

*Q. The in-batch negatives are free: they are the other pairs the batch already contains. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. A batch of B pairs gives B² pairs of which B are correct, and the rest cost nothing — which is why the method scales with the size of the batch.

*Q. A batch of 32 pairs gives how many image–caption pairs, of which how many are correct? — numeric (core)***

Answer: 1024

Why: 32 squared is 1,024 pairs, of which 32 are the correct ones and 992 are negatives — free, because the batch already contained them.

Go and do it

The loss, the gradient, and the retrieval, with the temperature and the batch size exposed. Open Train the contrastive model in the multimodal-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §clip:2.1 The contrastive objective — The loss, the in-batch negatives, and the temperature.

The words this lesson uses

  • The contrastive loss — The paired image and caption should be closer than the other pairs in the batch.
  • The in-batch negatives — The other pairs in the batch, used as things not to match.
  • The temperature — How sharp the distribution over the batch is.

Lesson 2. The data and the batch

What the scale of the pretraining buys

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what the number of pairs does to the retrieval
  • Explain why a larger batch gives more negatives and a better estimate
  • Describe the precomputation that makes the index affordable

The ideas

  • More pairs is more supervision, and the retrieval improves with it.
  • A larger batch is more negatives for the same cost, and a better estimate.
  • The document vectors never change, so the index is a matrix and the search is a matrix product.

Practice

*Q. Why can the document vectors be computed once and stored? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Because a document’s embedding does not depend on what is being retrieved
  • Because the encoder is small
  • Because the training has finished
  • Because the index is approximate

Correct.

Why: So the index is a matrix and the search is a matrix product — which is what makes a corpus of billions affordable.

*Q. In the contrastive image–text training, what does a larger batch buy? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • A longer context for the text encoder
  • ✓ More negatives, and therefore a better estimate of what the model must tell apart
  • A smaller embedding space
  • Less precomputation for the index

Correct — the batch is the discrimination task.

Why: The training asks each image to find its own caption among the batch’s candidates. A larger batch gives more negatives and a better estimate of the discrimination the model is being asked to learn — and the scale of the pretraining data is what makes the estimate worth having.

Go and do it

The retrieval against the batch size and against the number of pairs. Open Scale the batch and the data in the multimodal-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §clip:3 Results — The zero-shot transfer, and the size of the pretraining dataset.

The words this lesson uses

  • The in-batch negatives — The other pairs in the batch, used as things not to match.
  • Retrieval — Finding the caption that belongs with an image, among all of them.

2. The Modality Gap

Two spaces that are close, and not the same space

The images and the captions end up in one space, and the space is not quite symmetric. The gap, and the zero-shot classifier that works anyway.

Learning outcomes

  • Define the modality gap and say how it is measured
  • Describe the zero-shot classifier, and the part the prompt plays in it
  • Explain why the classifier works at all, given the gap

Lesson 3. The modality gap

One space, and a seam down the middle of it

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define the gap and say how it is measured
  • Explain what it means for a retrieval that works
  • Say what closing it would cost

The ideas

  • The images and the captions end up in one space, but the two halves are further apart than either half is from itself.
  • A retrieval works anyway, because the pairs are close even though the spaces are not.
  • So the gap is a property of the representation, not a failure of the method.

Practice

*Q. What is the modality gap? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The two modalities are further apart in the shared space than either is from itself
  • The two encoders have different numbers of parameters
  • The training data has more images than captions
  • The retrieval is inaccurate

Correct.

Why: A retrieval works anyway, because the pairs are close even though the two spaces are not.

*Q. What is the modality gap in a trained contrastive image–text model? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • The difference in dimensionality between the image and text encoders
  • ✓ Image embeddings and text embeddings occupy one shared space, but cluster in two separable regions of it
  • The distance between an image and its own caption, which training drives to zero
  • A bug in the normalisation of the embeddings

Correct — close spaces, not the same space.

Why: The images and the captions end up in one space, and the space is not quite symmetric: the two modalities cluster in separable regions. The gap is measurable — and the zero-shot classifier works anyway, which is the interesting part.

Go and do it

The within-modal and the between-modal similarities, and the gap between them. Open Measure the gap in the multimodal-lab application.

Where this came from

  • §clip:2 Method — The encoders, and the precomputation that makes the index affordable.

The words this lesson uses

  • The modality gap — The two modalities are further apart than either is from itself.
  • The embedding space — The space the encoders put things in.

Lesson 4. Zero-shot

Classifying with the class names and nothing else

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the zero-shot classifier and why it works at all
  • Say what part the prompt plays, and measure what it is worth
  • Explain the connection to the retrieval the model was trained for

The ideas

  • The class names are embedded with the text encoder, and the image is assigned to the closest of them.
  • The model was never trained to classify; it was trained to match a caption, and the class names are captions.
  • The prompt is part of the method, and a different template gives a different score.

Practice

*Q. Why does the zero-shot classifier work at all? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Because a class name is a caption, and the model was trained to match captions to images
  • Because the model was trained to classify
  • Because the embeddings are normalised
  • Because the batch contained the classes

Correct.

Why: The classifier is a retrieval against a set of captions that happen to be the class names.

*Q. In the zero-shot classifier, what part does the prompt play? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • None; the class names alone determine everything
  • ✓ The class names are embedded as captions — and the wording wrapped around them changes the embedding, measurably
  • It provides the gradients that adapt the encoder
  • It selects which encoder layer to read out

Correct — the prompt is doing retrieval’s job in classification’s clothing.

Why: The zero-shot classifier embeds each class name as if it were a caption and takes the nearest image embedding — the connection to the retrieval the model was trained for. The part the prompt plays is measurable: the wrapper sentence is worth real accuracy.

Go and do it

The zero-shot accuracy, and what each prompt template is worth. Open Classify with the names in the multimodal-lab application.

3. Instruction Tuning

Getting better at instructions, and what it costs

The recipe that turns a model into an assistant, and the tax it pays on everything it was good at before.

Learning outcomes

  • Describe the three stages of the recipe
  • Measure the alignment tax, and say what it is a tax on
  • Explain why the tax is a fact about training rather than a defect of the method

Lesson 5. The instruction recipe

Three stages, and what each one is for

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Describe the three stages of the recipe
  • Say what the visual instruction tuning adds to it
  • Explain why the stages are in that order
  • Say what the projection changes about a visual token, and what it costs

The ideas

  • The stages are: align the model to instructions, then teach it to read images, then tune it on visual instructions.
  • Each stage is a different kind of data, and the order is what makes the last one work.
  • The projection is a learned linear map from the vision width to the language width; it changes the width of a token, not its count.
  • The model that comes out is a different model from the one that went in.

Practice

*Q. What does instruction tuning do? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ Tunes the model on instructions and their answers, so that it follows instructions
  • Trains the model from scratch on instructions
  • Changes the tokenizer
  • Makes the model multimodal

Correct.

Why: And the model that comes out is a different model from the one that went in — which is the next lesson.

*Q. A 1024-wide vision token is projected to 4096 dimensions by a linear layer with a bias. How many parameters does the layer have? — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 4198400

Why: 1024 × 4096 = 4,194,304 entries in the matrix, plus 4096 bias terms, is 4,198,400. The number of tokens does not appear: the same matrix projects 576 tokens or four.

*Q. Few-shot learning puts the examples in the context rather than in the weights. — boolean (hard)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes — a different mechanism from fine-tuning, and a different bill, which is why the two are reported separately.

Go and do it

The gain on the instructions and the tax on everything else, as the tuning is strengthened. Open Run the recipe in the multimodal-lab application.

  • §llava:2 The method — Instruction tuning on visual data, and the three stages of the recipe.

The words this lesson uses

  • Instruction tuning — Tuning a model on instructions and the answers to them.
  • The alignment tax — What the instruction tuning gives up on the tasks it was good at.

Lesson 6. The alignment tax

What the tuning takes away

Estimated study time: 24 minutes

What you will learn

  • Define the alignment tax and say what it is measured on
  • Measure the gain and the tax, and the ratio between them
  • Explain why the tax is a fact about training and not a defect of the method

The ideas

  • Tuning on instructions makes the model better at instructions and slightly worse at what it was good at.
  • The tax is a measurement on the original task, before and after — not a claim.
  • And it is a consequence of the training, which means it is something the training can be made to avoid.

Practice

*Q. What is the alignment tax? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The accuracy the model gives up on its original task, measured before and after the tuning
  • The cost of running the tuning
  • The size of the instruction dataset
  • A failure of the method

Correct.

Why: It is a measurement on the original task, and the ratio between the gain and the tax is the number a practitioner is shopping for.

*Q. What is the honest reading of the alignment tax? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • A defect of the instruction-tuning method, removable with better code
  • ✓ A fact about training: tuning on instructions makes the model better at instructions and slightly worse at what it was good at
  • Evidence that the base model was badly trained
  • An artefact of evaluating with the wrong metric

Correct — the tax is measured on the original benchmark, and the gain is measured on the new one.

Why: The tax is a ratio: the gain on the instructed task against the loss on the original one. It is a fact about training — the model’s capacity is being reallocated — and the honest report states both numbers and the ratio between them.

Go and do it

The gain, the tax, and the ratio between them. Open Pay the tax in the multimodal-lab application.

  • §flamingo:2 The method — The interleaved sequence, and the few-shot learning it buys.

The words this lesson uses

  • The alignment tax — What the instruction tuning gives up on the tasks it was good at.
  • Instruction tuning — Tuning a model on instructions and the answers to them.

4. The Loss and the Bridge

What the objective normalises, and what the method holds still

Two later answers to the same recipe: a loss that decides each pair on its own, an architecture that freezes both towers and trains only the small part between them, and a resampler that bounds the visual token count.

Learning outcomes

  • Say what the softmax normalises, and show that the sigmoid loss does not normalise it
  • Measure the coupling between a pair and the rest of its batch
  • Say what is trained in a frozen-encoder bridge, and read its parameter bill
  • Explain how a fixed set of latents bounds the number of visual tokens

Lesson 7. The sigmoid loss

One decision per pair, and no denominator

Estimated study time: 26 minutes

What you will learn

  • Say what the softmax normalises and what that couples together
  • Read the same row of a batch under both losses
  • Explain what the bias balances, and why its value depends on the batch

The ideas

  • The softmax turns each row of the batch into a distribution, so one pair’s loss depends on every other pair.
  • The sigmoid loss is a sum of independent pair decisions, and a pair’s loss is a function of that pair alone.
  • The bias is the count of negatives, written as a probability; it is learned, but its starting point is a fact about the batch.

Practice

*Q. What does the sigmoid loss remove from the contrastive objective? — multiple-choice (core)***

  • ✓ The normalisation over the batch
  • The image encoder
  • The negatives
  • The temperature

Correct.

Why: Each pair is a logistic decision of its own, so the loss of one pair no longer contains a term from every other pair in the batch.

*Q. Appending an unrelated pair to the batch leaves the sigmoid loss of an existing pair exactly unchanged. — boolean (core)***

Answer: True

Why: Yes. The pair’s loss is a function of its own similarity, its label and the two learned constants. The softmax loss of its row, by contrast, changes, because the denominator has grown.

*Q. With a scale of 10, a bias of 0 and a similarity of 0, what is the sigmoid loss of one pair? (Three decimal places.) — numeric (hard)***

Answer: 0.693 ± 0.001

Why: The logit is 0, and −log σ(0) = log 2 ≈ 0.693. The label does not matter at zero: a positive and a negative pair are equally undecided.

Go and do it

Append unrelated pairs to the batch and watch one loss move while the other does not. Open Break the coupling in the multimodal-lab application.

  • §siglip:4.8 The negative-to-positive ratio — What the loss does as the unmatched pairs come to outnumber the matched ones.
  • §siglip:4.9 The bias term — The learned bias, and the initialisation that matches it to the size of the batch.

Further reading

  • Zhai et al., “Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training” — the paper this lesson is built on; the loss and the batch experiments are in §3 and §4.

The words this lesson uses

  • The sigmoid loss — Every pair is a yes-or-no question, decided on its own.
  • Coupling — The dependence of one pair’s loss on the rest of the batch.
  • The bias of the loss — The learned offset b that decides how likely a match is at zero similarity.
